1. INTRODUCTION
The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia
across enterprise archives, digital libraries, and oper-
ational repositories demands information retrieval sys-
tems capable of searching records that are not natively
textual. Transforming scanned documents and images
into queryable digital assets is essential for business
intelligence, compliance auditing, and decision support
[1]. However, real-world document ingestion faces severe
operational challenges: optical scanning introduces char-
acter substitutions and word fragmentation, while human
search queries frequently employ synonyms, paraphrases,
or shorthand rather than exact document text.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [2] addresses
the hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models
(LLMs) by grounding responses in retrieved domain
documents. Recently, multimodal extensions of RAG
have emerged to handle non-textual data, as surveyed
by Abootorabi et al. [3]. For example, Patel et al. [4]
and Joshi et al. [5] presented enterprise multimodal RAG
pipelines combining OCR ingestion, multimodal embed-
dings, and LLM reasoning. Concurrently, native vision-
language document retrievers like ColPali [6] index raw
document pixels with multi-vector late interaction.
While foundational studies in information retrieval—
notably Kantor and Voorhees [7] in the TREC-5 Con-
fusion Track and McNamee and Mayﬁeld [8] on char-
acter n-gram indexing—demonstrated the intrinsic noise
resilience of sub-word representations on degraded text,
their ﬁndings have not been systematically reconciled
with modern dense bi-encoders, neural cross-encoder
cascades, and document-native vision-language models
under semantic query variation.

2. RELATED WORK
A. Multimodal Representation and Retrieval
Early cross-modal retrieval systems relied on dual-
encoder contrastive learning. Models like CLIP [17] and
SigLIP [16] project images and text into a shared latent

ImageBind [18] extended this paradigm across six modal-

eﬀective for broad semantic matching, dual-encoders
compress multimedia into ﬁxed-dimension vectors, fre-

B. Multimodal RAG and Document Analysis
Integrating multimodal inputs into RAG workﬂows
has advanced rapidly with Vision-Language Models
(VLMs) and document foundation models. Document
retrievers such as ColPali [6] and M3DocRAG [21],
benchmarked on the ViDoRe suite [6] and DocVQA
[13], index document pages using multi-vector vision-
language representations (e.g., Qwen2-VL [22]) to bypass
OCR. A paradigm comparison is presented in Table I.
While promising, multi-vector representations require
substantial GPU memory and cross-attention compute.
Conversely, enterprise systems [4], [5] mediate retrieval
through text proxies. Our work evaluates this trade-oﬀ:
systematically delineating where text proxies excel and
where native visual representations remain necessary.
C. Character Subwords and OCR Degradation in In-
formation Retrieval
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems trans-
late document imagery into text, but routinely intro-
duce character substitutions, insertions, deletions, and
bounding-box permutations [10], [23]. Foundational in-
formation retrieval studies have long investigated textual
degradation. In the TREC-5 Confusion Track, Kantor
and Voorhees [7] systematically evaluated retrieval on
scanned, OCR-corrupted collections (at 5% and 20%
error rates), establishing known-item retrieval benchmarks
under optical corruption. Complementing this, McNamee
and Mayﬁeld [8] established that overlapping character
n-gram tokenization (e.g., 4–5grams) provides language-
neutral retrieval that rivals word-level tokenization while
providing intrinsic robustness to morphological variations
and spelling distortions. Early image-domain mitigation
strategies, including Otsu thresholding [24] and Hough
transforms [25] for skew correction, focused on image-
domain preprocessing. Our regime analysis builds upon
this foundation by evaluating character subwords against
modern dense bi-encoders, neural rerankers, and native vi-
sion models across commercial, LSTM, and neural OCR
architectures under controlled optical blur and semantic
variation.
D. Modern Dense and Learned Sparse Retrieval Models
Dense bi-encoders encode queries and passages in-
dependently [26], [27]. Recent architectures have ex-
panded this paradigm: multilingual dense models such
as BGE-M3 [28] support multi-granularity representa-
tions; learned sparse models like SPLADE [29] ex-
pand queries and documents into vocabulary-space term
weights; and late-interaction multi-vector architectures
like ColBERTv2 [30] preserve token-level interactions
at reduced latency. We position standard bi-encoders

3. REFERENCE RETRIEVAL ARCHITECTURE
The reference Multi-Stage Multimodal RAG architec-
ture is structured into four functional phases (Fig. 1):
(1) Ingestion and Preprocessing, (2) Hybrid Dense-Sparse
First-Stage Retrieval, (3) Neural Cross-Encoder Rerank-
ing and Cascade Escalation, and (4) Context Assembly.
A. Ingestion and Preprocessing Pipeline
Unstructured enterprise multimedia are mediated
through textual proxies. Proxies can be extracted across
modalities via OCR text [10], vision-language captions
[37], [38], [39], and speech transcripts [40].
• Documents and Forms: Administrative forms and
receipts are processed through document decompo-
sition, optional Otsu binarization [24] and Hough
skew correction [25], extracting text Td and bound-
ing boxes via OCR engines (Apple Vision [9],
Tesseract 5.5 [10], or EasyOCR [11]).
• Photographs: Natural photographs are indexed via
machine captions alongside native visual embed-
dings (CLIP [17], SigLIP [16]).
•
Acoustic Media: Continuous audio is transcribed
using Whisper [40] or embedded using contrastive
audio representations (CLAP [41]).
Dense embeddings are generated via Sentence-
BERT (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) [26] and BGE
(bge-base-en-v1.5) [27], while lexical tokens
are indexed with BM25 [19], [20]. The benchmark
uses in-memory indexes without external database
dependencies for exact reproducibility.

C. Uniﬁed Query Slices
To isolate semantic abstraction from optical noise,
queries are structured into four canonical slices:
1) Verbatim Lookups: Exact textual substrings ex-
tracted from documents (100% token overlap),
representing known-item search.
2) Light Paraphrases: Lexical substitutions and en-
tity rewrites (41.2% mean token overlap; e.g., sub-
stituting “dinner bill” for “total payable”), testing
semantic abstraction.
3) Answerable Factual Questions: Natural interrog-
atives preserving key factual and topical anchors
(e.g., “What was the total payment at Book Ta
K?”), testing real-world question answering.
4) Legacy Token-Stripped Probes: Probes where
shared lexical tokens are deliberately removed,
used strictly for conformal risk stress-testing.
Unless noted otherwise, evaluation queries for SROIE and
FUNSD were synthesized using gpt-4o-mini [46] at
temperature T = 0.0 (seed 42) with strict single ground-
truth answer resolution. DocVQA queries are 100%
human-authored. For MS-COCO (N = 1,000 Karpathy
test images), retrieval evaluates zero-shot text-to-image
ranking: exactly 1 held-out caption per image (Caption 3,
held out from candidate pool) serves as the query against
the 1,000-image candidate pool.

B. Micro-Mechanisms of Dense Collapse and Query
Formulation Controls
To isolate why dense vector representations collapse
under proxy corruptions while sparse inverted indexes en-
dure, we analyzed three underlying mechanisms (Fig. 4):
1) WordPiece Tokenization Fragmentation: As
character corruption increases from 0% to 40%,

sequence length truncation, we evaluated token length
distributions across all 626 SROIE receipts. While only

yields identical MRR to unchunked single-vector retrieval
(MiniLM: 0.2030 chunked vs. 0.2056 unchunked; BGE-
base: 0.3028 chunked vs. 0.3022 unchunked), demonstrat-
ing that sequence truncation is not the primary cause of
dense collapse.

8. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this work, we have established that intermediate
textual proxies in multimodal retrieval-augmented gen-
eration exhibit well-deﬁned, regime-dependent eﬃcacy
boundaries rather than uniform success or failure. Our
empirical investigation across 1,626 multimodal items
reveals three principal architectural insights:
First, lexical inverted indexing over character sub-
words (n-grams of length 3–5) provides a resilient
sparse retrieval foundation, outperforming word tokeniza-
tion across both commercial neural OCR and open-
source Tesseract under heavy optical blur (Apple Clean:
0.9436 vs. 0.8371; Degraded: 0.8248 vs. 0.6972; Tesser-
act: 0.8412 vs. 0.7364). This dominance reverses under
entity-substituting light paraphrases, where Word BM25
(0.4334) surpasses Character BM25 (0.2427). Second,
the collapse of dense bi-encoders on document text is
associated with a query-span formulation mismatch rather
than sequence truncation; structuring queries as natural

I. INTRODUCTION
The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia across
enterprise archives, digital libraries, and operational repos-
itories demands information retrieval systems capable of
searching records that are not natively textual. Transforming
scanned documents into queryable digital assets is essential
for business intelligence, compliance auditing, and decision
support [4]. However, real-world document ingestion faces
severe operational challenges: optical scanning introduces
character substitutions and word fragmentation, while human
search queries frequently employ synonyms, paraphrases, or
shorthand rather than exact document text.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [3] addresses the
hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models (LLMs)
by grounding responses in retrieved domain documents. Re-
cently, multimodal extensions of RAG have emerged to handle
non-textual data, as comprehensively surveyed by Abootorabi

II. RELATED WORK
A. Multimodal Representation and Retrieval
Early cross-modal retrieval systems relied on dual-encoder
contrastive learning. Models like CLIP [7] and SigLIP [8]
project images and text into a shared latent space using
sigmoid or softmax cross-entropy objectives. ImageBind [6]
extended this paradigm across six modalities (images, text,
video, audio, depth, and thermal) using images as the central
binding modality. While effective for broad semantic match-
ing, dual-encoders compress multimedia into ﬁxed-dimension
vectors, frequently losing granular lexical and structural to-
kens. Our hybrid design combines dense embeddings with
sparse lexical representations such as BM25 [9] to retain
both semantic intent and exact token matches. Unlike single-
modality dual-encoders that discard ﬁne-grained lexical iden-
tiﬁers, our framework analyzes the complementary regime
boundaries where character-level sparse indexing outperforms
dense representations under optical noise.
B. Multimodal RAG and Document Analysis
Integrating multimodal inputs into RAG workﬂows has
gained rapid momentum with the emergence of Vision-
Language Models (VLMs) and advanced LLMs. Recent native
multimodal document retrievers such as ColPali [25] and
M3DocRAG [26], benchmarked on the Visual Document

Retrieval (ViDoRe) suite [25], index document pages using
multi-vector vision-language representations to bypass optical
character recognition. A paradigm comparison is presented in
Table I. While promising, multi-vector VLM representations
require substantial GPU memory and heavy cross-attention
compute during query serving. Conversely, enterprise systems E.
such as Patel et al. [2] and Joshi et al. [5] mediate retrieval
through grounded text proxies, combining OCR document
ingestion, multimodal embeddings, and LLM generation. Our
work investigates this text-proxy paradigm: we evaluate the
empirical trade-offs of hybrid dense–sparse fusion, candidate
scoring, and iterative query decomposition, systematically
delineating where text proxies excel and where native visual
representations remain necessary. Unlike ColPali [25] which
5
mandates multi-vector VLM computation for every candidate
page regardless of query complexity, our regime analysis es-
tablishes the empirical conditions under which sub-millisecond
CPU text proxies match or exceed native vision models,
identifying when GPU-heavy inference is truly justiﬁed.
C. Multi-Hop Reasoning in Retrieval Systems
Multi-hop retrieval addresses queries where no single doc-
ument contains the complete answer [11], [13]. While multi-
hop text RAG systems (such as Baleen [11] and Self-Ask [12])
have established iterative query reformulation methods, multi-
hop retrieval across heterogeneous multimodal collections re-
mains less systematically evaluated. Our diagnostic targets the
case in which the second-hop keyword is absent from the
original query and must be recovered from ﬁrst-hop proxy
context; it does not claim that all multimodal QA benchmarks
assume co-located evidence. Unlike prior multi-hop pipelines
that rely on expensive generative LLMs for every hop, we
empirically show that rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance
feedback achieves parity in retrieval reachability with zero
generative token latency or API cost.

D. Adaptive Fusion, Cascade Ranking, and Selective Rerank-
ing
In information retrieval, static fusion coefﬁcients fail to
account for query-level variance. Query Performance Predic-
tion (QPP) [28] and adaptive fusion techniques dynamically
adjust interpolation weights between sparse and dense scores
based on query ambiguity or lexical speciﬁcity. Similarly,
cascade ranking architectures [29], [30] balance retrieval
efﬁciency and ranking precision by passing top candidates or
through successively more expressive models. In monomodal of
web search, cascades evaluate candidates using ﬁxed score et
thresholds or supervised early-exit classiﬁers. However, ex-
isting cascade rankers do not account for multimodal proxy
corruption (e.g., OCR or ASR transcription noise) or cross-
modal query routing. As summarized in Table II, we formulate as
and empirically evaluate candidate mechanisms—including
surface-feature query routing, conﬁdence-margin cascades
(∆1,2 < τmargin), and observable proxy reliability discounting
(rm(d))—to determine whether lightweight heuristic defenses

E. Optical Character Recognition Quality and Information
Retrieval
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems translate
physical document imagery into digital character sequences,
but practical scanning routinely introduces character substi-
tutions, insertions, deletions, and bounding-box permutations
[14], [17]. Foundational information retrieval studies have long
investigated the impact of textual degradation. In the TREC-
5 Confusion Track, Kantor and Voorhees [41] systematically
evaluated retrieval on scanned, OCR-corrupted collections (at
5% and 20% character error rates), demonstrating that OCR
noise degrades word-level matching and establishing known-
item retrieval benchmarks under optical corruption. Comple-
menting this, McNamee and Mayﬁeld [42] established that
overlapping character n-gram tokenization (e.g., 4–5grams)
provides language-neutral retrieval that rivals or exceeds word-
level tokenization while providing intrinsic robustness to mor-
phological variations and spelling distortions. Early image-
domain mitigation strategies, including Otsu thresholding [15]
and Hough transforms [16] for skew correction, focused on
image-domain preprocessing to boost OCR accuracy. How-
ever, in downstream information retrieval, post-OCR lexical
degradation leads to subword tokenization fragmentation in
subword-based language models and word omissions in lexical
indexes. Unlike prior works that treat OCR error as an unmod-
eled uniform noise channel, our regime analysis systematically
evaluates character n-gram representations against word-level
BM25 and neural cross-encoders across commercial, LSTM,
and neural OCR architectures under controlled optical blur.
F. Conformal Prediction and Risk-Controlled Cascades
In mission-critical information retrieval, deploying neural
cross-encoders or multi-vector Vision-Language Models for
to every candidate query imposes unsustainable serving latency
and energy expenditure. Cascade ranking pipelines address
this bottleneck by evaluating candidates through tiered stages,
escalating to expressive neural models only when preliminary
scores indicate ranking ambiguity [29], [30]. However, con-
ventional cascade systems rely on empirical score margins
or heuristic thresholds that offer no formal statistical control
of error rates. Conformal prediction, formulated by Bates
et al. [36] and surveyed by Angelopoulos and Bates [37], pro-
vides a distribution-free, ﬁnite-sample framework for bounding
user-speciﬁed risk metrics without restrictive distributional
assumptions. By framing the decision to escalate candidates
as a risk-controlling prediction problem, conformal prediction
enables retrieval systems to bound the expected marginal
probability of unescalated retrieval errors below a pre-speciﬁed
tolerance α. In this work, we ground production cascade rank-
ing in ﬁnite-sample marginal conformal risk control, bounding

the expected marginal miss rate while reducing computational
costs.
III. REFERENCE RETRIEVAL FRAMEWORK
The reference Multi-Stage Multimodal RAG architecture
is structured into four functional phases (Fig. 1): (1) Het-
erogeneous Multimodal Ingestion and Preprocessing, (2) Hy-
brid Dense-Sparse First-Stage Retrieval, (3) Neural Candidate
Reranking and Cascade Escalation, and (4) Multi-Hop Cross-
Modal Reasoning.
A. Heterogeneous Ingestion and Preprocessing Pipeline
To process unstructured enterprise multimedia, our archi-
tecture mediates retrieval through grounded textual proxies.
Proxies can be extracted across modalities via OCR text [17], d,
vision-language captions [22], and speech transcripts [18].
This design deliberately separates modality-speciﬁc extraction
from the common retrieval layer.
1. Scanned Document and Form Ingestion: Administra-
tive forms and receipts are processed through document page
decomposition, optional Otsu binarization [15] and Hough-
transform skew correction [14], [16], extracting text Td and
bounding boxes via OCR engines (such as Apple Vision
or Tesseract [17]). 2. Photographic Imagery: Natural pho-
tographs are indexed via descriptive machine captions (e.g.,
BLIP [22], BLIP-2 [38], Florence-2 [39]) alongside native
visual embeddings (CLIP [7], SigLIP [8]). 3. Acoustic Media:
Continuous audio recordings are transcribed using speech-to-
text models such as Whisper [18] or embedded directly using
contrastive audio-language representations (CLAP [1]).
Processed text representations are stored in a
dual layout: dense embeddings are generated via
Sentence-BERT (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) [21] and BGE
(bge-base-en-v1.5) [34], while lexical tokens are
indexed with BM25 [9], [43]. Milvus [19] and HNSW [20]
are compatible deployment choices, but the ofﬂine benchmark
scripts use an in-memory BM25 index and a dense embedding
matrix; no external vector database service is required for the
reported measurements.

To evaluate the empirical boundaries of text-proxy retrieval
without annotation leakage, we benchmarked an expanded
public multimodal collection under a rigorous pre-speciﬁed
experimental protocol across held-out evaluation splits. We
structure our evaluation across three canonical operational
regimes:
• Regime A (Text-Dominated): Scanned receipts and ad-
ministrative forms evaluated under real optical character
recognition (ICDAR 2019 SROIE [31] and FUNSD [33]),
isolating sub-word lexical dominance, micro-mechanisms
of dense collapse, and production reranking cascades.
• Regime B (Visual-Dominated): Photographic scene
search under synthetic caption proxies (N = 1,000 MS-
COCO Karpathy test images [32]), establishing where na-
tive vision-language embeddings signiﬁcantly outperform
machine-generated text representations.
• Regime C (Cross-Modal and Multi-Hop): Composi-
tional relational queries spanning modalities, establishing
where rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance feedback
matches iterative generative LLM bridging without API
overhead.
Preliminary feasibility pilots over internal personal album pho-
tos and synthetic noise sweeps are documented in Appendix A.

V. LIMITATIONS AND THREATS TO VALIDITY
To facilitate objective peer assessment, we document the
critical limitations of this study:
1) Benchmark domain concentration: Our primary text
retrieval evaluations focus predominantly on a sin-
gle document-type family (retail receipts from SROIE,
N = 626) alongside scanned administrative forms from
FUNSD (N = 100) and natural images from MS-COCO
(N = 1,000). While receipt and form structures capture
common real-world OCR artifacts, document layouts
with multi-column prose, rich typography, or complex
ﬁnancial tables may exhibit differing degradation dy-
namics.
2) Cross-engine and cross-domain OCR generalization:
While Apple Vision represents an advanced commer-
cial neural OCR system, replication across open-source
Tesseract 5.5 LSTM and deep neural EasyOCR 1.7.2
conﬁrms that our headline ﬁndings (character n-gram re-
silience on verbatim optical noise and dense bi-encoder
collapse) replicate across distinct OCR architectures.
However, the ordering under light paraphrases exhibits
domain sensitivity: on retail receipts with entity sub-
stitutions, Word BM25 outperforms character BM25

4) Answerable question formulation: Our answerable
questions evaluate natural factual queries isolating se-
mantic abstraction from lexical absence. However, real-
world user queries may exhibit broader syntactic and

5) LLM judge bias and audit sample size: Automated
diagnostic scoring uses gpt-4o-mini [23], which car-
ries documented biases [24]. Mitigated by dual-reviewer
human auditing rated by the two co-authors (A. K. Ven-

faithfulness, 0.8926 relevance, 0.9451 correctness, mean
κ = 0.9031). While inter-annotator agreement is high,
expanding audits to external non-author panels remains
desirable.

6) Multi-hop retrieval utility and exploratory power
limits: Query decomposition incurs a 45% latency
penalty (4,736.8 ms vs. 3,260.0 ms). Paired discordant
analysis across 50 multi-hop queries indicates that multi-
hop LLM bridging provides no statistically detectable
retrieval improvement over single-stage hybrid retrieval
(+1 net hit / 50; exact McNemar p = 1.000) or single-
stage dense retrieval (identical 32/50 hits). However,

7) Dose-response non-linearity: The retrieval drop under
query mismatch is non-monotonic across query types:
light paraphrases with entity substitutions trigger severe
drops (Apple Vision ∆= 0.4037 MRR; Tesseract
∆= 0.3400), whereas answerable factual questions

8) Synthetic vs. optical noise divergence: Character n-
gram robustness and dictionary-based reliability weight-
ing tuned on synthetic character permutations fail to
translate directly to real optical OCR blur. System ar-
chitects must validate on physical optical degradation
rather than synthetic character noise.
9) LLM-generated query synthesis and single gen-
erator threat: Evaluation queries for light para-
phrases and answerable questions were synthesized us-
ing gpt-4o-mini [23]. No human-authored query set
was used. Because queries were generated using a single
LLM without multi-model cross-generation or human
validation, model-generated queries may under-represent
human typographical errors, spontaneous colloquialisms,
or ambiguous intent.
10) Dense and learned sparse model scope: Our evaluation
benchmarks representative widely deployed bi-encoders
(all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge-base-en-v1.5).
Emerging models with multilingual subword tokenizers
(e.g., BGE-M3), learned sparse representations
(SPLADE), and token-level multi-vector text interaction
(ColBERTv2) represent compelling extensions for
future benchmark iterations.
VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this work, we have established that intermediate textual
proxies in multimodal retrieval-augmented generation exhibit
well-deﬁned, regime-dependent efﬁcacy boundaries rather than
uniform success or failure. Our empirical investigation across
1,626 multimodal items (SROIE, FUNSD, MS-COCO) reveals
three principal architectural insights.
First, lexical inverted indexing over character sub-words (n-
grams of length 3–5) provides a resilient sparse retrieval foun-
dation, outperforming standard word tokenization across both
commercial neural OCR and open-source Tesseract engines
under heavy optical blur (Apple Clean: 0.9436 vs. 0.8371;

to 78.4% escalation; an equal-escalation ﬁxed margin achieves
matching MRR (0.3579 vs. 0.3577). On the 50-query multi-
hop diagnostic suite, extractive PRF shows no detectable
difference from generative LLM bridging (Hit@10 0.640 vs.
0.640, p = 1.000; formal equivalence not established) with
zero API cost.
Future research will extend this regime framework along
three axes: (1) expanding held-out evaluation to multilingual
and handwritten administrative archives; (2) designing adap-
tive conformal thresholding conditioned on real-time query
difﬁculty estimators; and (3) investigating sparse-guided se-
lective caching for vision-language models. By formalizing
the trade-offs between computational overhead and represen-
tation ﬁdelity, this work provides an engineering roadmap
for efﬁcient, trustworthy multimodal retrieval in real-world
computing systems.

I. INTRODUCTION
The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia across
enterprise archives, digital libraries, and operational repos-
itories demands information retrieval systems capable of
searching records that are not natively textual. In enterprise
document workﬂows—such as healthcare systems digitizing
millions of paper patient intake records, legal ﬁrms archiving
scanned court proceedings, and supply chain enterprises in-
dexing procurement invoices—organizations process massive
volumes of unstructured physical records daily. Transforming
these documents into queryable digital assets is essential
for business intelligence, compliance auditing, and decision
support [4]. However, real-world document ingestion faces
severe operational challenges: optical scanning introduces
character substitutions and word fragmentation, while human
search queries frequently employ synonyms, paraphrases, or
shorthand rather than exact document text.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [3] addresses the
hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models (LLMs)
by grounding responses in retrieved domain documents. Re-
cently, multimodal extensions of RAG have emerged to handle
non-textual data, as comprehensively surveyed by Abootorabi

In a proxy-mediated design, three practical failure modes
remain important:
1) Single-Stage Dense Retrieval Pitfalls: Relying ex-
clusively on single-stage dense vector similarity per
a
turn can induce semantic drift. Dense embeddings may
overlook exact lexical tokens, numerical identiﬁers, item
codes, and proper nouns that sparse inverted indexes can
match directly [9].
2) Absence of Candidate Score Recalibration: A bi-
encoder score alone does not expose token-level agree-
ment with a candidate’s proxy text. A lightweight
second-stage scorer can therefore be useful before con-
text assembly, even when it is not a neural cross-encoder.
3) Failure on Multi-Hop Queries Across Modalities: A
single retrieval pass does not ensure that a fact recovered
from one modality becomes a useful probe for another.
Iterative bridging can improve lexical reachability, but it
also introduces cascading extraction errors that must be
of measured rather than assumed away.
To investigate these trade-offs, this paper presents a public-
benchmark regime analysis of text-proxy retrieval across held-
out evaluation splits1.

II. RELATED WORK
A. Multimodal Representation and Retrieval
Early cross-modal retrieval systems relied on dual-encoder
contrastive learning. Models like CLIP [7] and SigLIP [8]
project images and text into a shared latent space using
sigmoid or softmax cross-entropy objectives. ImageBind [6]
extended this paradigm across six modalities (images, text,
video, audio, depth, and thermal) using images as the central
= binding modality. While effective for broad semantic match-
ing, dual-encoders compress multimedia into ﬁxed-dimension
vectors, frequently losing granular lexical and structural to-
kens. Our hybrid design combines dense embeddings with
sparse lexical representations such as BM25 [9] to retain
both semantic intent and exact token matches. Unlike single-
modality dual-encoders that discard ﬁne-grained lexical iden-
tiﬁers, our framework analyzes the complementary regime
boundaries where character-level sparse indexing outperforms
dense representations under optical noise.
B. Multimodal RAG and Document Analysis
Integrating multimodal inputs into RAG workﬂows has
gained rapid momentum with the emergence of Vision-
Language Models (VLMs) and advanced LLMs. Recent native
multimodal document retrievers such as ColPali [26] and
M3DocRAG [27], benchmarked on the Visual Document
Retrieval (ViDoRe) suite [36], index document pages using
multi-vector vision-language representations to bypass optical
character recognition. While promising, multi-vector VLM
representations require substantial GPU memory and heavy
cross-attention compute during query serving. Conversely,
enterprise systems such as Patel et al. [2] and Joshi et al. [5]
mediate retrieval through grounded text proxies, combining
OCR document ingestion, multimodal embeddings, and LLM
generation. Our work investigates this text-proxy paradigm:
we evaluate the empirical trade-offs of hybrid dense–sparse
fusion, candidate scoring, and iterative query decomposition,
systematically delineating where text proxies excel and where
native visual representations remain necessary. Unlike ColPali
[26] which mandates multi-vector VLM computation for every
candidate page regardless of query complexity, our regime

analysis establishes the exact conditions under which sub-
millisecond CPU text proxies match or exceed native vision
models, identifying when GPU-heavy inference is truly justi-
ﬁed.
C. Multi-Hop Reasoning in Retrieval Systems
Multi-hop retrieval addresses queries where no single doc-
ument contains the complete answer [11], [13]. While multi-
hop text RAG systems (such as Baleen [11] and Self-Ask [12])
have established iterative query reformulation methods, multi-
hop retrieval across heterogeneous multimodal collections re-
mains less systematically evaluated. Our diagnostic targets the
F.
case in which the second-hop keyword is absent from the
original query and must be recovered from ﬁrst-hop proxy
context; it does not claim that all multimodal QA benchmarks
assume co-located evidence. Unlike prior multi-hop pipelines
that rely on expensive generative LLMs for every hop, we
empirically show that rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance
feedback achieves parity in retrieval reachability with zero
generative token latency or API cost.
D. Adaptive Fusion, Cascade Ranking, and Selective Rerank-
ing
In information retrieval, static fusion coefﬁcients fail to
account for query-level variance. Query Performance Predic-
tion (QPP) [29] and adaptive fusion techniques dynamically
adjust interpolation weights between sparse and dense scores
based on query ambiguity or lexical speciﬁcity. Similarly, to
cascade ranking architectures [30], [31] balance retrieval
efﬁciency and ranking precision by passing top candidates
through successively more expressive models. In monomodal
web search, cascades evaluate candidates using ﬁxed score
thresholds or supervised early-exit classiﬁers. However, ex-
isting cascade rankers do not account for multimodal proxy
corruption (e.g., OCR or ASR transcription noise) or cross-
modal query routing. As summarized in Table II, we formulate
and empirically evaluate candidate mechanisms—including
surface-feature query routing, conﬁdence-margin cascades
(∆1,2 < τmargin), and observable proxy reliability discounting
(rm(d))—to determine whether lightweight heuristic defenses
provide measurable utility over standard inverted indexes. Un-
like prior cascade ranking that relies on uncalibrated heuristic
margins, we ground cascade escalation in distribution-free A.
conformal risk control to guarantee test-set error bounds.
E. Optical Character Recognition Quality and Information A
Retrieval
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems translate
physical document imagery into digital character sequences,
but practical scanning routinely introduces character substi-
tutions, insertions, deletions, and bounding-box permutations it
[14], [17]. Foundational information retrieval studies have es-
tablished that standard word-level tokenizers (such as inverted
indexes using whitespace and punctuation delimiters) suffer
catastrophic vocabulary mismatch when typographical errors
fracture keyword strings. Early mitigation strategies, including

[COLUMN_BREAK]

Otsu thresholding [15] and Hough transforms [16] for skew
correction, focused on image-domain preprocessing to boost
OCR accuracy. However, in downstream information retrieval,
post-OCR lexical degradation leads to subword tokenization
fragmentation in subword-based language models and word
omissions in lexical indexes. Unlike prior works that treat
OCR error as an unmodeled uniform noise channel, our regime
analysis systematically evaluates character n-gram represen-
tations against word-level BM25 and neural cross-encoders
across both commercial and open-source OCR engines under
controlled optical blur.
F. Conformal Prediction and Risk-Controlled Cascades
In mission-critical information retrieval, deploying neural
cross-encoders or multi-vector Vision-Language Models for
every candidate query imposes unsustainable serving latency
and energy expenditure. Cascade ranking pipelines address
this bottleneck by evaluating candidates through tiered stages,
escalating to expressive neural models only when prelimi-
nary scores indicate ranking ambiguity [30], [31]. However,
conventional cascade systems rely on empirical score mar-
gins or heuristic thresholds that offer no formal statistical
guarantees on retrieval accuracy. Conformal prediction, for-
mulated by Bates et al. [37] and surveyed by Angelopoulos
to
and Bates [38], provides a distribution-free, ﬁnite-sample
framework for bounding user-speciﬁed risk metrics without
restrictive distributional assumptions. By framing the decision
to escalate candidates as a risk-controlling prediction problem,
conformal prediction enables retrieval systems to bound the
probability of unescalated retrieval errors strictly below a pre-
speciﬁed tolerance α. In this work, we ground production cas-
cade ranking in ﬁnite-sample marginal conformal risk control,
establishing rigorous mathematical miss-rate guarantees while
reducing computational costs.

IV. EMPIRICAL REGIME ANALYSIS OF SPARSE, DENSE,
AND NATIVE-VISUAL RETRIEVAL UNDER PROXY NOISE
B.
To evaluate the empirical boundaries of text-proxy retrieval
without annotation leakage, we benchmarked an expanded
public multimodal collection under a rigorous pre-speciﬁed
experimental protocol across held-out evaluation splits. We
structure our evaluation across three canonical operational
regimes:
• Regime A (Text-Dominated): Scanned receipts and ad-
ministrative forms evaluated under real optical character
recognition (ICDAR 2019 SROIE [32] and FUNSD [34]),
isolating sub-word lexical dominance, micro-mechanisms
of dense collapse, and production reranking cascades.
• Regime B (Visual-Dominated): Photographic scene
search under synthetic caption proxies (N = 1,000 MS-
COCO Karpathy test images [33]), establishing where
native vision-language embeddings decisively surpass
machine-generated text representations.
• Regime C (Cross-Modal and Multi-Hop): Composi-
tional relational queries spanning modalities, establishing
where rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance feedback
matches iterative generative LLM bridging without API
overhead.

relevance feedback as the primary bridging mechanism.
Extractive bridging matches iterative generative LLM
bridging in retrieval accuracy (Target Hit@10 = 0.820)

external API costs.

Document-native multi-vector models (ColQwen2)

latency (249.21 ms vs. 0.87 ms) and require ∼6 GB of
dedicated GPU VRAM. Conformal cascade ranking
enables systems to capture neural accuracy gains
while saving over 21% of compute overhead with
mathematically bounded risk.
V. LIMITATIONS AND THREATS TO VALIDITY
To facilitate objective peer assessment, we document the
critical limitations of this study:
1) Benchmark domain concentration: Our primary text
retrieval evaluations focus predominantly on a sin-
gle document-type family (retail receipts from SROIE,
N = 626) alongside scanned administrative forms from
FUNSD (N = 100) and natural images from MS-COCO
(N = 1,000). While receipt and form structures capture
common real-world OCR artifacts, document layouts
with multi-column prose, rich typography, or complex
ﬁnancial tables may exhibit differing degradation dy-
namics.
2) Cross-engine OCR generalization: While Apple Vi-
sion represents an advanced commercial neural OCR
system, replication across open-source Tesseract 5.5
LSTM conﬁrms that our architectural ﬁndings (character
n-gram robustness and dense collapse) replicate across
distinct OCR model architectures and error distributions.

VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this work, we have established that intermediate textual
proxies in multimodal retrieval-augmented generation exhibit
well-deﬁned, regime-dependent efﬁcacy boundaries rather than
uniform success or failure. Our empirical investigation across
1,626 multimodal items reveals three principal architectural
insights.
First, lexical inverted indexing over character sub-words
(n-grams of length 3–5) provides an extraordinarily resilient
sparse retrieval foundation, outperforming standard word to-
kenization across both commercial neural OCR and open-
source engines under heavy optical blur; whole-word and
dense encoders only surpass sub-word sparse matching when
search queries diverge into semantic paraphrases. Second,
the frequently observed collapse of dense bi-encoders on
administrative text reﬂects a query-span formulation mismatch
rather than sequence truncation; structuring user queries as
contextual answerable questions restores semantic discrim-
inability without modifying document vectors. Third, native
visual representations are indispensable for unconstrained pho-
tographic imagery, where automated caption proxies suffer se-
vere information bottlenecks; however, on structured document
pages, document-native vision-language models yield statisti-
cally indistinguishable accuracy from CPU lexical search on
factual questions while imposing two orders of magnitude
higher latency.
These ﬁndings directly challenge the emerging assump-
tion that end-to-end multi-vector vision models must uni-
versally replace OCR-mediated indexing. Instead, we show
that lightweight sub-word lexical inverted indexes on CPU
remain optimal for high-throughput verbatim and entity-centric
search, while cross-encoder cascades should be reserved selec-
tively for paraphrased queries via conformal risk control. Fur-
thermore, rule-based extractive entity bridging matches multi-
hop generative LLM techniques without incurring recurring
token latency or cloud API costs.
Future research will extend this regime framework along
three axes: (1) expanding held-out evaluation to multilingual
and handwritten administrative archives; (2) designing adap-
tive conformal thresholding conditioned on real-time query
difﬁculty estimators; and (3) investigating sparse-guided selec-
tive caching for vision-language models. By formalizing the
trade-offs between computational overhead and representation
ﬁdelity, this work provides a rigorous engineering roadmap
for efﬁcient, trustworthy multimodal retrieval in real-world
computing systems.

The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia
across enterprise archives, digital libraries, and operational
repositories demands information retrieval systems capa-

Modern knowledge workflows frequently require querying

recordings, and photographic archives—while preserving
exact names, identifiers, and category labels [4].
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [3] addresses
the hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models
(LLMs) by grounding responses in retrieved domain doc-
uments. Recently, multimodal extensions of RAG have
emerged to handle non-textual data, as comprehensively
surveyed by Abootorabi et al. [28]. For example, Patel et
al. [2] presented an enterprise multimodal RAG pipeline
employing an OCR document ingestion module, Image-

In a proxy-mediated design, three practical failure

1) Single-Stage Dense Retrieval Pitfalls: Relying exclu-

A single retrieval pass does not ensure that a

II. Related Work
A. Multimodal Representation and Retrieval
Early cross-modal retrieval systems relied on dual-
encoder contrastive learning. Models like CLIP [7] and
SigLIP [8] project images and text into a shared latent
space using sigmoid or softmax cross-entropy objectives.
ImageBind [6] extended this paradigm across six modali-
ties (images, text, video, audio, depth, and thermal) using
images as the central binding modality. While effective
for broad semantic matching, dual-encoders compress
multimedia into fixed-dimension vectors, frequently losing
granular lexical and structural tokens. Our hybrid design
combines dense embeddings with sparse lexical represen-
tations such as BM25 [9] to retain both semantic intent
and exact token matches.
B. Multimodal RAG and Document Analysis
Integrating multimodal inputs into RAG workflows has
gained rapid momentum with the emergence of Vision-
Language Models (VLMs) and advanced LLMs. Recent
native multimodal document retrievers such as ColPali
[26] and M3DocRAG [27], benchmarked on the Visual
Document Retrieval (ViDoRe) suite [36], index document
pages using multi-vector vision-language representations
to bypass optical character recognition. While promis-
ing, multi-vector VLM representations require substantial
GPU memory and heavy cross-attention compute during
query serving. Conversely, enterprise systems such as
Patel et al. [2] and Joshi et al. [5] mediate retrieval through
grounded text proxies, combining OCR document inges-
tion, multimodal embeddings, and LLM generation. Our
work investigates this text-proxy paradigm: we evaluate
the empirical trade-offs of hybrid dense–sparse fusion,
candidate scoring, and iterative query decomposition,
systematically delineating where text proxies excel and
where native visual representations remain necessary.

WASHINGTON, March 10.—The Inaugura-
tion, with all of its pomp and circumstance,
is over, and Grover Cleveland is now Presi-
dent of the United States. The daily press
has already given to the world the details of
the magnificence of the procession; the
brilliancy of the ball; and best of all the
manly tone and hopeful spirit of the inau-
gural address. The procession was by all
odds the largest and most imposing that has
ever attended the seating of a President;
and in dignity and impressiveness was not
unworthy of the coronation of a king.
There were over eight miles of marching
men; quite a hundred bands of music, em-
bracing not a few of the most celebrated of
the land, including the band of the Seventh
Regiment and Gilmore's great band of one
hundred performers. The procession re-
quired four hours to pass a given point. It
was very gratifying to see so many fine
looking and well equipped colored soldiers
in line and to note the many complimentary
remarks they elicited from the great crowd
that filled the streets. Never have the col-
ored soldiers made a handsomer appearance
and never have they been given better posi-
tions and treated with greater consideration
than in this procession to inaugurate a Dem-
ocrati, Fre ident. The local companies
turned out full ranks, led by the three com-
panies of the Washington Cadets in their
new overcoats, under the command of Major
C. A. Fleetwood. Their marching was sim-
ply perfect. Among the visiting companies
were the Baltimore Rifles, seventy men,
Capt. Geo. M. Matthews, who came in for a
large share of applause for their fine looks
and soldierly appearance. The South Caro-
lina volunteers from Charleston, accompa-
nied by Brig.-Gen. J. C. Clausen. The State
Guard of Richmond, Capt. R. A. Paul.
Baltimore City Guards, seventy men, Capt.
W. R. Spencer. Three companies from
Norfolk, Maj. W. H. Palmer, and one from
Fredericksburg, Va.
The Inaugural of President Cleveland
has pleased every one, and has gone far to
disarm any prejudice or apprehension enter-
tained against him, and all are now prepared
to give him and his administration a fair and
honest trial and to hope for the best. The
colored clerks in office, if not elated, are at
least serene and hopeful; and while it is too
early to predict what will be the outcome
all believe that the President is in earnest in
relation to civil service reform.
Never were so many persons drawn to the
city as by this occasion. It is stated that
the P. R. R. Co. alone brought in 300,000
persons. Quite a number of colored ladies

CHEYENNE, Wyo., July 23. — James
Averill and the notorious Cattle Queen
Kate Maxwell, were lynched by cowboys
Sunday night. The bodies of the “rus-
tier" and range queen dangled from the
same limb of a big cottonwood yesterday
morning. The scene of the lawless but
justifiable deed of the midnight riders is
on the Sweetwater river, in Carbon
County, near Independence Rock, a land-
mark made historical during the rush
overland to the California gold fields.
Averill was postmaster at Sweetwater.
Kate Maxwell was the heroine of a sensa-
papers throughout the country three

months ago, when she raided a gambling
house and recovered a large sum of money
won from her enployes.
Stockmen of the Sweetwater region
have been the victims of cattle thieves
for years. On account of the prejudice
against the large outfits, it has been im-
possible to convict on this charge, and
the rustlers have become very bold.
Averill and his remarkable partner have
been very active in thieving. The woman
could hold her own on the range, riding
like a demon, shooting on the slightest
pretext, and handling the lariat and
branding iron with the skill of a va-
quero.

The Necessity for the Meeting.
The unceasing energy of those bent
upon the creation of a public sentiment
adverse to the Afro-Americans. The
open advocacy by Senator Tillman, Gov-
ernor Vardaman, John Temple Graves
and others of the repeal of the Four-
teenth and Fifteenth Amendments to
the Federal Constitution, thus reducing
the Afro-Americans of the South to
serfdom: the timid and uncertain stand
of those who essay to befriend us, even
to President Roosevelt, who has said so
much about “fair play” and the “Door
of Hope" but who has dealt us a severe
blow in the dismissal of the colored sol-
diers of the 25th Infantry without an
adequate trial; the bold and defiant as-
saults of those satisfied with nothing
short of our absolute undoing, certainly
necessitates the meeting of the leaders
of the race in an advisory way. The
situation is grave and demands the ex-
ercise of wisdom, prudence, patience,
and intelligent effort to overcome the
dangers menacing what political and civil
rights we have left.

When Do Text Proxies Suffice? A Regime Analysis of Sparse,
Dense, and Native-Visual Retrieval Under Proxy Noise

Abstract: Multimodal retrieval systems often index textual proxies, such as OCR output or generated captions, instead of raw visual
media. We compare sparse lexical, dense text, and native-visual retrieval on receipts, document pages, and natural images. For
verbatim receipt lookup, character 3~Sgram BM25 outperforms word BM25 on Apple Vision clean OCR (MRR 0.9436 vs. 0.8371),
degraded OCR (0.8248 vs. 0.6972), and Tesseract clean OCR (0.8412 vs. 0.7364). Under synthetic entity-substituting paraphrases,
this ordering reverses (0.2427 vs. 0.4334 on gpt-40-mini), whereas under open-weight Qwen2.5-7B and human queries where
topical anchors are preserved, character and word BM25 perform comparably (0.5802 vs. 0.6292 and 0.5549 vs. 0.5766). ColQwen2
achieves MRR 0.4962 on the primary synthetic paraphrase set (compared with 0.4334 for word BM25), but was not evaluated
across secondary or human query sets. On a 500-query DocVQA subset, ColQwen2 reaches MRR 0.6450, while tested text-proxy
baselines reach at most 0.3507. On 1,000 MS-COCO images, SigLIP reaches MRR 0.6071, outperforming baseline BLIP captions
(0.3728) and detailed Florence-2 captions (0.4420; all p < 10~). Query formulation strongly affects dense retrieval: BGE-Base
MRR rises from 0.3256 on short snippets to 0.5263 on natural answerable questions. Results suggest selecting retrieval methods by
query type and modality. Generalization is limited by sampled benchmark subsets and the disclosed pretraining overlap for ColQwen2.

Keywords: Multimodal RAG, Text Proxies, Proxy Noise, Dense-Sparse Regime Analysis, Cascade Ranking, Conformal

Risk Control, Document Retrieval.

1. INTRODUCTION

The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia
across enterprise archives, digital libraries, and oper-
ational repositories demands information retrieval sys-
tems capable of searching records that are not natively
textual. Transforming scanned documents and images
into queryable digital ets is essential for business
intelligence, compliance auditing, and decision support
[1]. However, real-world document ingestion faces severe
operational challenges: optical scanning introduces char-
acter substitutions and word fragmentation, while human
search queries frequently employ synonyms, paraphrases,
or shorthand rather than exact document text.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [2] addresses
the hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models
(LLMs) by grounding responses in retrieved domain
documents. Recently, multimodal extensions of RAG
have emerged to handle non-textual data, as surveyed
by Abootorabi et al. [3]. For example, Patel et al. [4]
and Joshi et al. [5] presented enterprise multimodal RAG
pipelines combining OCR ingestion, multimodal embed-
dings, and LLM reasoning. Concurrently, native vision-
language document retrievers like ColPali [6] index raw
document pixels with multi-vector late interaction.

While foundational studies in information retrieval—
notably Kantor and Voorhees [7] in the TREC-5 Con-
fusion Track and McNamee and Mayfield [8] on char-
acter n-gram indexing—demonstrated the intrinsic noise
resilience of sub-word representations on degraded text,
their findings have not been systematically reconciled
with modern dense bi-encoders, neural cross-encoder
cascades, and document-native vision-language models
under semantic query variation.

To address this gap, this paper establishes an empir-

ical regime map of when text proxies suffice versus
when native representations are required across a pri-
mary benchmark of 1,626 multimodal items (626 scanned
retail receipts and 1,000 photographic scenes, plus ded-
icated transfer suites on forms and visual documents)
under frozen 50/50 evaluation splits’.

Key Contributions:

source Tesseract 5.5 LSTM [10], and deep neu-
ral EasyOCR 1.7.2 [11] (N = 306 held-out
probes, 813 corpus items), character 3—Sgram

+0.1276 degraded blur, +0.1048 clean Tesseract;
all prom < 10-4). We delineate its strict scope
boundary: this advantage reverses under synthetic
entity-substituting light paraphrases, where Word
BM25 outperforms Character BM25 (0.4334 vs.
0.2427). On receipts, document-native ColQwen2-
v1.0 [12] achieves 0.4962 MRR under paraphrases
(+0.0628 over Word BM25, prom = 0.0072) but

topical anchors, CPU lexical retrieval (Char BM25

forms ColQwen2 (0.8595; Real-OCR paired diff
+0.0733, Clean GT diff +0.0876, p = 0.00012,
Table II) while operating at 0.87 ms CPU verbatim

2) Dense Bi-Encoder Deficit Associated with
Query Formulation: We demonstrate that dense
bi-encoder collapse on document text is associ-

truncation constraints (real max_seq_length =

3) Native-Visual vs. Text-Proxy Representation
Boundaries: On photographic scenes (N = 1,000

4) Actionable Empirical Decision Guide for MM-
RAG Builders: We synthesize our experimental
findings across OCR engines, degradation levels,
and query formulations into an empirical deci-

and statistically indistinguishable sets across doc-
ument, image, and query regimes.

2. RELATED WORK
A. Multimodal Representation and Retrieval

Early cross-modal retrieval systems relied on dual-
encoder contrastive learning. Models like CLIP [17] and
SigLIP [16] project images and text into a shared latent

space using sigmoid or softmax cross-entropy objectives.
ImageBind [18] extended this paradigm acros: modal-
ities using images as the central binding modality. While
effective for broad semantic matching, dual-encoders
compress multimedia into fixed-dimension vectors, fre-
quently losing granular lexical and structural tokens. Hy-
brid retrieval designs frequently combine dense embed-
dings with sparse lexical representations such as BM25
[19], [20] in an effort to retain both broad semantic intent
and exact token matches, though our empirical findings
show that on OCR-degraded verbatim documents, optimal
convex fusion collapses to standalone sparse indexing
(@parse = 1-00).
B. Multimodal RAG and Document Analysis
Integrating multimodal inputs into RAG workflows
has advanced rapidly with Vision-Language Models
(VLMs) and document foundation models. Document
retrievers such as ColPali [6] and M3DocRAG [21],
benchmarked on the ViDoRe suite [6] and DocVQA
[13], index document pages using multi-vector vision-
language representations (e.g., Qwen2-VL [22]) to bypass
OCR. A paradigm comparison is presented in Table I.
While promising, multi-vector representations require
substantial GPU memory and cross-attention compute.
Conversely, enterprise systems [4], [5] mediate retrieval
through text proxies. Our work evaluates this trade-off:
systematically delineating where text proxies excel and
where native visual representations remain necessary.
C. Character Subwords and OCR Degradation in In-
formation Retrieval
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems trans-
late document imagery into text, but routinely intro-
duce character substitutions, insertions, deletions, and
bounding-box permutations [10], [23]. Foundational in-
formation retrieval studies have long investigated textual
degradation. In the TREC-5 Confusion Track, Kantor
and Voorhees [7] systematically evaluated retrieval on
scanned, OCR-corrupted collections (at 5% and 20%
error rates), establishing known-item retrieval benchmarks
under optical corruption. Complementing this, McNamee
and Mayfield [8] established that overlapping character
n-gram tokenization (e.g., 4-Sgrams) provides language-
neutral retrieval that rivals word-level tokenization while
providing intrinsic robustness to morphological variations
and spelling distortions. Early image-domain mitigation
strategies, including Otsu thresholding [24] and Hough
transforms [25] for skew correction, focused on image-
domain preprocessing. Our regime analysis builds upon
this foundation by evaluating character subwords against
modern dense bi-encoders, neural rerankers, and native vi-
sion models across commercial, LSTM, and neural OCR:
architectures under controlled optical blur and semantic
variation.
D. Modern Dense and Learned Sparse Retrieval Models
Dense bi-encoders encode queries and passages in-
dependently [26], [27]. Recent architectures have ex-
panded this paradigm: multilingual dense models such
as BGE-M3 [28] support multi-granularity representa-
tions; learned sparse models like SPLADE [29] ex-
pand queries and documents into vocabulary-space term
weights; and late-interaction multi-vector architectures
like CoIBERTv2 [30] preserve token-level interactions
at reduced latency. We position standard bi-encoders

E. Cascade Ranking and Conformal Risk Control

Cascade ranking architectures [32], [33] balance re-
trieval efficiency and precision by passing candidates
through tiered stages, escalating to expressive models
only when scores indicate ranking ambiguity. Conven-
tional cascade rankers rely on empirical thresholds with-
out formal statistical guarantees. Distribution-free risk-
controlling prediction sets, formulated by Bates et al. [34],
and conformal risk control, developed by Angelopoulos
et al. [35], [36], provide a finite-sample framework for
bounding user-specified risk metrics below a tolerance
a. In this work, we evaluate production cascade ranking
under marginal conformal risk control.

The reference Multi-Stage Multimodal RAG architec-

B. OCR Engines and Optical Degradation Conditions

Document text is extracted across three distinct OCR
engines:

1) Apple Vision Neural OCR [9]: Commercial neu-

ral OCR (VNRecognizeTextRequest).

2) Tesseract 5.5 LSTM OCR [10]: Standard open-
source LSTM OCR engine.

3) EasyOCR 1.7.2 Deep CRNN [11]: Deep neu-
ral OCR combining CRAFT text detection and
ResNet-CRNN recognition.

Documents are evaluated under: (1) Clean OCR, (2) Re-
alistic Optical Degradation (Gaussian blur 0 = 1.5,
bilinear 50% downscaling, random skew +2.5°, JPEG
compression Q = 20), and (3) Human Ground Truth text.
For both Word and Character 3-5gram BM25, hyperpa-
rameters are tuned on the Dev split (k; = 0.9,b = 0.5).
Word BM25 uses whitespace/punctuation tokenization,
lowercase normalization, and standard stopword removal
without stemming (to preserve exact part numbers and
serials). Character BM25 extracts overlapping 3-Sgrams
over lowercased strings preserving word boundaries, eval-
uated across the identical parameter grid.

C. Unified Query Slices

To isolate semantic abstraction from optical noise,

queries are structured into four canonical slices:

1) Verbatim Lookups: Exact textual substrings ex-
tracted from documents (100% token overlap),
representing known-item search.

2) Light Paraphrases: Lexical substitutions and en-
tity rewrites (41.2% mean token overlap; e.g., sub-
stituting “dinner bill” for “total payable”), testing
semantic abstraction.

3) Answerable Factual Questions: Natural interrog-
atives preserving key factual and topical anchors
(e.g., “What was the total payment at Book Ta
K?”), testing real-world question answering.

4) Legacy Token-Stripped Probes: Probes where
shared lexical tokens are deliberately removed,
used strictly for conformal risk stress-testing.

Unless noted otherwise, evaluation queries for SROIE and
FUNSD were synthesized using gpt-40-mini [46] at
temperature T = 0.0 (seed 42) with strict single ground-
truth answer resolution. DocVQA queries are 100%
human-authored. For MS-COCO (N = 1,000 Karpathy
test images), retrieval evaluates zero-shot text-to-image
ranking: exactly | held-out caption per image (Caption 3,
held out from candidate pool) serves as the query against
the 1,000-image candidate pool.

E. Evaluation Metrics and Statistical Testing

Systems are evaluated on Mean Reciprocal Rank
(MRR), Hit@k (k € {1,5,10}), and nDCG@10. Paired
differences are evaluated via two-tailed paired permuta-
tion tests (Nperm = 100,000 sign flips, empirical resolution
limit p = 10~>) with family-wise Holm-Bonferroni cor-
rection (pyoim) Structured across four pre-specified fami-
lies: Family | (sparse OCR comparisons, m = 4), Family
2 (ColQwen2 vs. text proxies across primary regimes,
m = 5), Family 3 (native vision vs. caption proxies on
COCO, m = 8), and Family 4 (architectural ablations,
m = 7). Confidence intervals (95% CI) are computed
via cluster bootstrap resampling at the document level
(10,000 iterations).
F. Hardware Serving Profiles

Sparse BM25 and bi-encoders are profiled on Apple
M2 (16GB RAM, batch size = 1, warm cache). Neural
cross-encoders and ColQwen2 are profiled on Nvidia
Tesla T4 GPU (14.56GB VRAM, batch size = 1, warm
cache). These represent environment-specific serving pro-
files, not a single-machine controlled benchmark; on the
matched GPU host CPU, BM25 lookup takes 0.96 ms,
whereas running ColQwen2 on CPU exceeds 8,000 ms
per query.

Formulation Controls

under proxy corruptions while sparse inverted indexes en-
dure, we analyzed three underlying mechanisms (Fig. 4):

1) WordPiece Tokenization Fragmentation: As
character corruption increases from 0% to 40%,

tiple subwords. Mean subwords per word escalates
from 1.347 (clean) to 1.774 (10% noise), 2.246
(20% noise), and 2.994 (40% noise, a +122.3%
increase).

mentation shifts contextual attention weights,
driving acute embedding drift. Relative to un-
corrupted text, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 mean docu-
ment embedding cosine similarity collapses from

To verify whether OCR degradation and retrieval

evaluated standardized character and word error rates via

native-visual and text-proxy retrieval across DocVQA
(Table IX), followed by multi-engine replication across
Apple Vision, Tesseract, and EasyOCR on SROIE and
FUNSD (Table X).

all N = 626 SROIE receipts, true character recognition
noise drops to CER = 0.1387 and WER = 0.2165
on clean receipts (a 51.3% reduction from concatenated
metrics), and CER = 0.3086 (WER = 0.4595) under
optical degradation. Across EasyOCR 1.7.2, line-aligned
recognition yields CER = 0.3250 (WER = 0.4983) on

Replication across EasyOCR 1.7.2 [11] confirms
that the retrieval hierarchy generalizes: under verbatim
queries, Character BM25 retains top MRR (0.8519 clean,

MRR from 0.8371 to 0.8005, confirming that fuzzy word

Visual Geometry Boundary on DocVQA: On the
DocVQA ViDoRe benchmark (N = 500 queries across
500 document pages with 100% human-authored ques-
tions, Table IX), text proxies fed by Tesseract 5.5 OCR
achieve MRR < 0.3507 (Word BM25: 0.3107, Char
BM25: 0.3141, Dense BGE: 0.2737, Hybrid: 0.3507). In
sharp contrast, document-native ColQwen2 [12] achieves
MRR = 0.6450 [95% CI: 0.601, 0.689] (Hit@10 =
0.8410, nDCG@10 = 0.6886 [0.646, 0.731]; published
ViDoRe leaderboard reports nDCG@5 = 0.6120). We
note that the ColPali/ColQwen2 architecture incorporates
DocVQA training splits within its ViDoRe training mix-
ture, whereas the text proxy baselines are zero-shot and
off-the-shelf. Even with this caveat, the substantial perfor-
mance gap demonstrates that native pixel representations
substantially outperform generic text proxies when visual
layout and 2D spatial geometry govern answerability.

Query Formulation Dynamics across LLMs and
Human Queries: As documented in Table XI, evaluating

6)

an open-weight generator (Qwen2 .5-7B, evaluated across
all N = 306 test probes) alongside authentic human-
authored queries (V = 100 and N = 200) refines the
boundary conditions of the sparse reversal and dense
deficit. Under primary synthetic queries (gpt-40-mini),
aggressive entity stripping and synonym substitution
caused Character BM25 to collapse below Word BM25
(0.2427 vs. 0.4334). However, under Qwen2.5-7B and
human queries, where contextual and vendor anchors
are naturally preserved, Character BM25 closely tracks
Word BM25 (0.5802 vs. 0.6292 on Qwen2.5; 0.5549
vs. 0.5766 on human N = 200). This indicates that the
Character-to-Word BM25 reversal is specifically driven
by entity-substitution paraphrasing rather than generalized
paraphrasing. Furthermore, the dense bi-encoder deficit
markedly attenuates under human formulation: BGE-
base MRR rises from 0.1601 on synthetic entity-stripped
queries to 0.4909 on human queries (N = 200) and
0.5020 (N = 100), confirming that dense collapse is
predominantly driven by query formulation mismatch
rather than intrinsic vocabulary failure.

Cross-Domain Generalization on FUNSD Forms:
On 100 scanned administrative forms from FUNSD [45]
(Table X), Character BM25 maintains high verbatim ac-
curacy (0.8433 Apple, 0.8066 Tesseract), showing no sta-
tistically significant difference from Word BM25 (0.8364
Apple, diff +0.0069, p > 0.05; 0.7763 Tesseract). Un-
der light paraphrasing, Word BM25 drops to 0.1573,
while Character BM25 achieves 0.2228 (diff +0.0655,
p = 0.012), Dense BGE achieves 0.1834 (diff +0.0261,
p = 0.084), and Hybrid reaches 0.2099, confirming that
sub-word indexing and dense matching offer resilience
against vocabulary mismatch on complex semi-structured
forms.

ColQwen2 Retrieval on Document Receipts: Bench-
marking ColQwen2-v1.0 [12] on document images on
Tesla T4 GPU yields 0.4962 MRR [95% CI: 0.4484,
0.5472] under light paraphrasing (+0.0628 over Word
BM25 0.4334, prom = 0.0072; +0.0627 over Tuned Hy-
brid 0.4335, pHoim = 0.0095). Conversely, on natural an-
swerable factual questions with preserved topical anchors,
CPU lexical retrieval decisively outperforms ColQwen2
on held-out receipts (Char BM25 0.9471 Clean GT /
0.9328 Apple Clean vs. ColQwen2 0.8595; diff +0.0876,
p = 0.00012, Table II). Under artificial entity-abstracted
controls, both sparse and native-visual models collapse to
mutual floor performance ( 0.05 MRR; ColQwen2 0.0546
vs. Char BM25 0.0495, diff +0.0051, prom = 1.0000;
formal TOST equivalence with A = +0.05 holds trivially
due to near-zero scores).

A. Ablation of Regime-Aware Multimodal Proxy

domain terminology.

zero detectable lift under real Apple Vision OCR.

8. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

In this work, we have established that intermediate
textual proxies in multimodal retrieval-augmented gen-
eration exhibit well-defined, regime-dependent efficacy
boundaries rather than uniform success or failure. Our
empirical investigation across 1,626 multimodal items
reveals three principal architectural insights:

First, lexical inverted indexing over character sub-
words (n-grams of length 3-5) provides a resilient
sparse retrieval foundation, outperforming word tokeniza-
tion across both commercial neural OCR and open-
source Tesseract under heavy optical blur (Apple Clean:
0.9436 vs. 0.8371; Degraded: 0.8248 vs. 0.6972; Tesser-
act: 0.8412 vs. 0.7364). This dominance reverses under
entity-substituting light paraphrases, where Word BM25
(0.4334) surpasses Character BM25 (0.2427). Second,
the collapse of dense bi-encoders on document text is
associated with a query-span formulation mismatch rather
than sequence truncation; structuring queries as natural

answerable questions improves BGE-Base MRR from
0.3256 to 0.5263 on identical document text. Third,
native visual representations strongly outperform ma-
chine caption proxies for natural photographs (SigLIP
MRR 0.6071 vs. machine captions 0.3728, p < 10-4),
approaching 5-reference human gold captions within a
narrow statistical margin (0.6071 vs. 0.6210, diff —0.0139,
paired p = 0.321; formally equivalent at A = +0.05
with prosr = 0.0050, 90% CI [—0.0369, +0.0091]); on
visual document pages (DocVQA), native ColQwen2
substantially outperforms generic text proxies (0.6450 vs.
< 0.3507); however, on standard receipts with natural
answerable queries, CPU lexical retrieval (Char BM25
0.9471) outperforms ColQwen2 (0.8595, p = 0.00012)
while imposing 0.87—-5.72 ms CPU latency vs. 249.21 ms
GPU latency.

In exploratory cascade risk calibration, marginal con-
formal prediction achieved 58.5% empirical split coverage
against the 0.05 nominal risk target (82.0% for high-
probability RCPS), demonstrating that marginal calibra-
tion does not provide conditional risk coverage under
entity shifts and performs comparably to a simple fixed-
margin baseline (MRR 0.3579 vs. 0.3577). On expanded
relational multi-hop queries (NV = 100), extractive PRF
is formally equivalent to generative LLM bridging under
TOST (Hit@ 10 0.820 vs. 0.820, prosr = 0.0062 < 0.01 at
A = £0.05) while eliminating 394x LLM latency and API
cost. By formalizing the trade-offs between computational
overhead and representation fidelity, this work provides an
engineering roadmap for efficient, trustworthy multimodal
retrieval in real-world computing systems.

RAG) frequently indexes textual proxies over raw pixels. Eval-
uating a 1,626-item benchmark under frozen 50/50 Dev/Test
splits (N. = 306 test probes, 813 items), we delineate when
proxies suffice and when native representations are indispensable.
On verbatim lookups, character 3-Sgram BM25 outperforms

Pttom < 10“), reversing under entity rewrites (0.2427 vs. 0.4334).
On documents, native ColQwen?2 achieves 0.4962 MRR under

at 249.21ms on Tesla T4 GPU vs. 0.87ms CPU lookups. On
DocVQA (N = 500), ColQwen2 (0.6450) substantially outper-
forms text proxies (< 0.3507). Dense bi-encoder deficit is asso-
ciated with query formulation mismatch; answerable questions
improve BGE-Base MRR to 0.5263 (Hit@ 10 79.74%). Conformal
cascade calibration achieves mean test miss risk 0.0494 on

beats machine captions (0.3728, p < 10~*) with no significant
difference detected from human gold captions (p = 0.142). In

Index Terms—Multimodal RAG, Text Proxies, Proxy Noise,
Dense-Sparse Regime Analysis, Cascade Ranking, Conformal

I. INTRODUCTION

The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia across
enterprise archives, digital libraries, and operational repos-
itories demands information retrieval systems capable of
searching records that are not natively textual. Transforming
scanned documents into queryable digital assets is essential
for business intelligence, compliance auditing, and decision
support [4]. However, real-world document ingestion faces
severe operational challenges: optical scanning introduces
character substitutions and word fragmentation, while human
search queries frequently employ synonyms, paraphrases, or
shorthand rather than exact document text.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [3] addresses the
hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models (LLMs)
by grounding responses in retrieved domain documents. Re-
cently, multimodal extensions of RAG have emerged to handle
non-textual data, as comprehensively surveyed by Abootorabi

et al. [27]. For example, Patel et al. [2] presented an enterprise
multimodal RAG pipeline employing an OCR document in-
gestion module, ImageBind embeddings indexed in a Milvus
vector database, and fine-tuned LLaMA-3.

To establish rigorous engineering guidance for proxy-
mediated retrieval, this investigation addresses four founda-
tional empirical questions:

1) Query Formulation vs. Document Representation:
Under what conditions does semantic abstraction (para-
phrasing, natural interrogatives) vs. verbatim lexical
matching dictate the crossover point between sparse
lexical and dense semantic retrieval?

OCR Engine Architecture and Optical Degradation:
How do commercial neural OCR (Apple Vision) and
open-source LSTM OCR (Tesseract 5.5) interact with
character sub-word vs. whole-word inverted indexing
under pristine text and heavy optical blur?
Native-Visual vs. Text-Proxy Representations: When
do intermediate text proxies suffice for enterprise search,
and under what specific query and visual conditions do
document-native multi-vector models (ColQwen2) and
visual encoders (SigLIP) justify their GPU memory and
latency cost:
Computational Budgeting and Risk-Controlled Esca-
lation: Can confidence margins and finite-sample con-
formal prediction provide bounded risk control to prune
expensive neural cross-encoders while preserving top-
rank precision?

To investigate these trade-offs, this paper presents a public-
benchmark regime analysis of text-proxy retrieval across held-
out evaluation splits!.
