C. Multi-Hop Reasoning in Retrieval Systems
Multi-hop retrieval addresses queries where no single doc-
ument contains the complete answer [11], [13]. While multi-
hop text RAG systems (such as Baleen [11] and Self-Ask [12])
have established iterative query reformulation methods, multi-
hop retrieval across heterogeneous multimodal collections re-
mains less systematically evaluated. Our diagnostic targets the
case in which the second-hop keyword is absent from the
original query and must be recovered from first-hop proxy
context; it does not claim that all multimodal QA benchmarks
assume co-located evidence. Unlike prior multi-hop pipelines
that rely on expensive generative LLMs for every hop, we
empirically show that rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance
feedback achieves parity in retrieval reachability with zero
generative token latency or API cost.
D. Adaptive Fusion, Cascade Ranking, and Selective Rerank-
ing
In information retrieval, static fusion coefficients fail to
account for query-level variance. Query Performance Predic-
tion (QPP) [28] and adaptive fusion techniques dynamically
adjust interpolation weights between sparse and dense scores
based on query ambiguity or lexical specificity. Similarly,
cascade ranking architectures [29], [30] balance retrieval
efficiency and ranking precision by passing top candidates
through successively more expressive models. In monomodal
web search, cascades evaluate candidates using fixed score
thresholds or supervised early-exit classifiers. However, ex-
isting cascade rankers do not account for multimodal proxy
corruption (e.g., OCR or ASR transcription noise) or cross-
modal query routing. As summarized in Table II, we formulate
and empirically evaluate candidate mechanisms-including
surface-feature query routing, confidence-margin cascades
(41,2 < Tmargin), and observable proxy reliability discounting
(rm (d))-to determine whether lightweight heuristic defenses
provide measurable utility over standard inverted indexes. Un-
like prior cascade ranking that relies on uncalibrated heuristic
margins, we ground cascade escalation in distribution-free
conformal risk control to bound expected test-set error rates.
E. Optical Character Recognition Quality and Information
Retrieval
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems translate
physical document imagery into digital character sequences,
but practical scanning routinely introduces character substi-
tutions, insertions, deletions, and bounding-box permutations
[14], [17]. Foundational information retrieval studies have long
investigated the impact of textual degradation. In the TREC-
5 Confusion Track, Kantor and Voorhees [41] systematically
evaluated retrieval on scanned, OCR-corrupted collections (at
5% and 20% character error rates), demonstrating that OCR
noise degrades word-level matching and establishing known-
item retrieval benchmarks under optical corruption. Comple-
menting this, McNamee and Mayfield [42] established that
overlapping character n-gram tokenization (e.g., 4-5grams)
provides language-neutral retrieval that rivals or exceeds word-
level tokenization while providing intrinsic robustness to mor-
phological variations and spelling distortions. Early image-
domain mitigation strategies, including Otsu thresholding [15]
and Hough transforms [16] for skew correction, focused on
image-domain preprocessing to boost OCR accuracy. How-
ever, in downstream information retrieval, post-OCR lexical
degradation leads to subword tokenization fragmentation in
subword-based language models and word omissions in lexical
indexes. Unlike prior works that treat OCR error as an unmod-
eled uniform noise channel, our regime analysis systematically
evaluates character n-gram representations against word-level
BM25 and neural cross-encoders across commercial, LSTM,
and neural OCR architectures under controlled optical blur.
F. Conformal Prediction and Risk-Controlled Cascades
In mission-critical information retrieval, deploying neural
cross-encoders or multi-vector Vision-Language Models for
every candidate query imposes unsustainable serving latency
and energy expenditure. Cascade ranking pipelines address
this bottleneck by evaluating candidates through tiered stages,
escalating to expressive neural models only when preliminary
scores indicate ranking ambiguity [29], [30]. However, con-
ventional cascade systems rely on empirical score margins
or heuristic thresholds that offer no formal statistical control
of error rates. Conformal prediction, formulated by Bates
et al. [36] and surveyed by Angelopoulos and Bates [37], pro-
vides a distribution-free, finite-sample framework for bounding
user-specified risk metrics without restrictive distributional
assumptions. By framing the decision to escalate candidates
as a risk-controlling prediction problem, conformal prediction
enables retrieval systems to bound the expected marginal
probability of unescalated retrieval errors below a pre-specified
tolerance a. In this work, we ground production cascade rank-
ing in finite-sample marginal conformal risk control, bounding

the expected marginal miss rate while reducing computational
costs.
III. REFERENCE RETRIEVAL FRAMEWORK
The reference Multi-Stage Multimodal RAG architecture
is structured into four functional phases (Fig. 1): (1) Het-
erogeneous Multimodal Ingestion and Preprocessing, (2) Hy-
brid Dense-Sparse First-Stage Retrieval, (3) Neural Candidate
Reranking and Cascade Escalation, and (4) Multi-Hop Cross-
Modal Reasoning.
A. Heterogeneous Ingestion and Preprocessing Pipeline
To process unstructured enterprise multimedia, our archi-
tecture mediates retrieval through grounded textual proxies.

Proxies can be extracted across modalities via OCR text [17],

This design deliberately separates modality-specific extraction
from the common retrieval layer.

Continuous audio recordings are transcribed using speech-to-

IV. EMPIRICAL REGIME ANALYSIS OF SPARSE, DENSE,
AND NATIVE-VISUAL RETRIEVAL UNDER PROXY NOISE
To evaluate the empirical boundaries of text-proxy retrieval
without annotation leakage, we benchmarked an expanded
public multimodal collection under a rigorous pre-specified
experimental protocol across held-out evaluation splits. We
structure our evaluation across three canonical operational
regimes:
• Regime A (Text-Dominated): Scanned receipts and ad-
ministrative forms evaluated under real optical character
recognition (ICDAR 2019 SROIE [31] and FUNSD [33]),
isolating sub-word lexical dominance, micro-mechanisms
of dense collapse, and production reranking cascades.
• Regime B (Visual-Dominated): Photographic scene
search under synthetic caption proxies (V = 1,000 MS-
COCO Karpathy test images [32]), establishing where na-
tive vision-language embeddings significantly outperform
machine-generated text representations.
• Regime C (Cross-Modal and Multi-Hop): Composi-
tional relational queries spanning modalities, establishing
where rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance feedback
matches iterative generative LLM bridging without API
Preliminary feasibility pilots over internal personal album pho-
tos and synthetic noise sweeps are documented in Appendix A.
A. Benchmark Scale, Partitions, and Optical Degradation
Pipeline
The public benchmark integrates 626 authentic scanned
receipt documents from ICDAR 2019 SROIE [31] and 1,000
photographic distractors from MS-COCO [32], establishing
a corpus of 1,626 pooled multimodal items and 612 factual
probes. To prevent data snooping, the corpus is partitioned
into a strict 50/50 Dev/Test split by Item ID:
• Dev Split (N = 306 probes, 813 corpus items):
Dedicated strictly to hyperparameter tuning (e.g., hybrid
fusion coefficient a*, visual weight y*, and conformal
risk thresholds +*).
• Held-Out Test Split (N = 306 probes, 813 corpus
items): Frozen for evaluation across Seeds 42, 43, and
44 with zero test-split tuning.
Document text representations are extracted using Apple's
Vision framework (VNRecognizeTextRequest) under
two distinct conditions: (1) Clean OCR, yielding normalized
character error rate (CER) = 0.2848 and word error rate
(WER) = 0.3928 under standardized document-level Leven-
shtein alignment [40]; and (2) Realistic Optical Degradation,
applying Gaussian blur (o = 1.5), bilinear 50% downscaling,
random skew (12.5°), and aggressive JPEG re-compression
(Q = 20), elevating CER to 0.3822 and WER to 0.5691.
Queries are evaluated across three prompt variations generated
by an independent LLM at T = 0.0 (gpt-40-mini [23]):
verbatim lookups (100% token overlap), natural light para-
phrases (41.2% mean token overlap), and natural answerable
questions (preserving key factual anchors while enforcing
natural interrogative phrasing).

Numeric-Heavy probes (MiniLM MRR = 0.033, BGE =

BGE = 0.135). Conversely, character n-gram BM25
retains high accuracy across all buckets: Numeric-Heavy

To verify whether this dense degradation is an artifact
of sequence length truncation, we evaluated token length
distributions across all 626 SROIE receipts. While only 4
receipts (0.64%) exceed 512 tokens, the real parameter limit
for al1-MiniLM-L6-v2 is max_seq_length = 256, where
209 of 626 receipts (33.39%) exceed 256 WordPiece tokens.
However, evaluating chunked MaxP retrieval across 150-word
sliding windows (where no chunk exceeds 256 tokens) yields
identical MRR to unchunked single-vector retrieval (MiniLM:
0.2030 chunked vs. 0.2056 unchunked; BGE-base: 0.3028
chunked vs. 0.3022 unchunked), demonstrating that sequence
truncation is not the primary cause of dense collapse.

G. Regime C: Cross-Modal Relational Reasoning and Multi-
Hop Retrieval
To evaluate whether multi-hop query decomposition pro-
vides measurable retrieval utility over single-stage retrieval,
we conducted an exploratory paired discordant analysis across
the 50 diagnostic multi-hop queries (Table IX).
The MM-RAG pipeline beat single-stage hybrid retrieval on
only 2 queries (mh_35, mh_50) and lost on 1 query (mh_25),
yielding a net advantage of only +1 hit out of 50 queries
(TargetHit@10 = 0.640 vs. 0.620; exact two-tailed McNemar
p = 1.0000). Compared to single-stage dense retrieval, the
MM-RAG pipeline achieved identical performance (32/50 hits;
McNemar p = 1.0000). While multi-hop LLM bridging
outperforms sparse BM25 alone (+8 net hits; p = 0.0215),
it introduces a 45% latency penalty (4,736 ms vs. 3,260 ms)
without providing statistically detectable retrieval lift over
single-stage hybrid or dense baselines.
Furthermore, as shown in Table X, grounded extractive
pseudo-relevance feedback achieves identical TargetHit@10
(0.640 vs. 0.640 multi-hop, exact McNemar p = 1.0000,
paired difference 0.0000 [95% CI: -0.0792, +0.0792]), re-
covering intermediate reachability without generative API
latency or hallucinations. On the 50 diagnostic multi-hop
queries, the 95% bootstrap confidence interval for paired Tar-
get Hit@10 difference [-0.0792, +0.0792] spans beyond the
10.05 equivalence margin; thus, formal statistical equivalence
is not shown, and we report no detectable difference between
extractive and generative bridging. With N = 50 paired
queries, statistical power is limited (the minimum detectable
difference at a = 0.05 and 80% power exceeds 10.0792),
meaning this comparison is strictly exploratory. Crucially, the
pooled 100-query metric (Hit@10 = 0.8200) cannot serve as
statistical support for multi-hop parity, as it aggregates 50
trivial single-hop controls where both methods achieve 100%
hit rate with zero discordant pairs.
To evaluate generation quality and retrieval correctness, the
N = 110 case packet was evaluated under dual-reviewer
auditing rated by the two co-authors (A. K. Vennela and G.
S. B. Koushik) blinded to model IDs and hypothesis targets.
This audit confirmed high inter-rater agreement: faithfulness
k = 0.8716 (95.45% observed agreement), query relevance
k = 0.8926 (96.36% agreement), and media correctness
k = 0.9451 (98.18% agreement), establishing an overall
consensus of mean k = 0.9031.
H. Cross-Engine OCR Replication and Error Characteriza-
tion
To verify that the empirical retrieval hierarchy does not
depend on proprietary Apple Vision preprocessing, we repli-
cated the retrieval benchmarks using open-source Tesseract 5.5
LSTM OCR across 626 SROIE receipts (Table XIII). Evalu-
ating full-document Levenshtein edit distance via standard-
ized JWER 40] reveals the true transcription quality: clean
Tesseract achieves CER = 0.2939 and sequence WER =
0.4879, explaining why character 3-5gram BM25 retains high
retrieval accuracy (MRR = 0.8412). Under realistic optical
blur, Tesseract error escalates to CER = 0.6377 and WER =
0.8063.
As shown in Table XII, we evaluate both sequence Lev-
enshtein WER (WERseq) and a multiset error rate (MERBow);
note that the latter is not a standard sequence WER, but evalu-
ates bag-of-words multiset symmetric difference: MERBow =
Cer (w) -Cmp(w). While sequence WERseq = S+D+1 aligns
token order and counts an OCR character error as a single
token substitution (S = 1), multiset evaluation penalizes that
same error as both a reference omission (D = 1) and an
inserted out-of-vocabulary artifact (I = 1). When severe OCR
corruption splits or mangles words into out-of-vocabulary
fragments, multiset symmetric differences escalate sharply
(e.g., reaching 0.5919 clean and 1.0043 degraded blur on
Tesseract), although on clean Apple Vision OCR where word
boundaries remain largely intact, multiset error is lower than
sequence Levenshtein WER (0.2476 vs. 0.3928).
Quantifying retrieval performance
against human-
transcribed ground truth exposes the exact degradation
gradient imposed by proxy noise: on verbatim lookups, clean
Apple Vision OCR drops 0.0411 MRR vs. ground-truth text
(0.9443 vs. 0.9854 for Char BM25), clean Tesseract drops
0.1442 MRR (0.8412 vs. 0.9854), and degraded optical
blur on Tesseract drops 0.5845 MRR (0.4009 vs. 0.9854).
Across both engines, character 3-5gram BM25 retains
top MRR under verbatim lookups (0.9443 Apple, 0.8412

To confirm that this empirical retrieval hierarchy generalizes
beyond Apple Vision and Tesseract, we further replicated
retrieval across EasyOCR 1.7.2 (CRAFT neural detector +

As detailed in Table XII, clean EasyOCR achieves CER =
0.4026 and WER = 0.5684 (escalating to CER = 0.7755
and WER = 0.9827 under blur). Across both clean and
degraded conditions, the hierarchy replicates consistently: un-
der verbatim queries, Character 3-5gram BM25 retains top
MRR (0.8519 clean, 0.4272 degraded blur) over Word BM25
(0.7649 clean, 0.3472 degraded blur; PHolm < 10-4), revers-

0.3792 vs. Character BM25 0.2292 clean), while dense bi-
encoders suffer severe deficits (MiniLM MRR = 0.1549 clean).
Furthermore, evaluating Levenshtein edit-distance expansion
on Word BM25 fails to close the gap (MRR drops from 0.8371
to 0.8005 on clean Apple Vision), confirming that fuzzy word
expansions induce spurious matches across corpus distractors
rather than matching sub-word structure. Finally, evaluating
visual document retrieval on the Doc VA ViDoRe benchmark
(N = 500 queries across 500 document pages, Table XI)
exposes the boundary of text proxies on rich visual forms:
while text proxies fed by Tesseract 5.5 OCR achieve MRR
≤ 0.3507 (Word BM25: 0.3107, Char BM25: 0.3141, Dense

achieves MRR = 0.6450 [95% CI: 0.601, 0.689] (Hit@10 =

indispensable when visual geometry governs answerability.

To provide an engineering reference for system architects
balancing retrieval accuracy against computational overhead,
Table XV reports runtime latency, memory footprint, and index
storage across evaluated retrieval architectures profiled on their

While ColQwen2 provides superior semantic generalization
on visual documents, it incurs 249.21 ms mean query latency
(P95: 270.45 ms) and demands 5,964.7 MB GPU memory. In
contrast, standalone character 3-5gram BM25 requires under
1 ms mean latency (0.87 ms on verbatim lookups; 5.72 ms on
answerable queries) and only 4.2 MB index storage on CPU,
offering orders of magnitude lower resource utilization.
Finally, synthesizing all empirical experiments across
modalities, noise conditions, and query types, Table XVI
presents an actionable retrieval architecture decision guide.
I. Practical Implications and Production Deployment Guide-
lines
To translate our empirical findings into actionable engi-
neering recommendations for system architects and retrieval
engineers, Table XVI synthesizes four core deployment rules:
1) For Document Search System Architects: For ad-
ministrative receipts, invoices, and standard scanned
forms, character 3-5gram BM25 serves as the default
primary retrieval engine under verbatim and entity-
centric queries. It provides MRR > 0.84 on clean
Apple Vision and Tesseract 5.5 OCR at 0.87 ms CPU
latency, outperforming neural bi-encoders without GPU
infrastructure. Neural cross-encoder reranking should be
triggered selectively only when user queries exhibit low
lexical overlap with document metadata.
2) For Photographic and Image-Centric Archives: Na-
tive vision-language embeddings (e.g., SigLIP or CLIP)
are strongly preferred for natural photograph search.
On MS-COCO (N = 1,000), machine-generated cap-
tion proxies achieve MRR 0.3728 vs. SigLIP 0.6071
(p < 10-4), a substantial information loss. Human gold
captions reach 0.5835 (no significant difference detected
from SigLIP, p = 0.142; equivalence not tested).
3) For Multi-Hop Relational Reasoning: Rule-based ex-
tractive pseudo-relevance feedback shows no detectable
retrieval difference from iterative generative LLM bridg-
ing on the 50-query exploratory diagnostic suite (Target
Hit@10 0.640 vs. 0.640, exact McNemar p = 1.000;
formal equivalence not established as the 95% CI
[-0.0792, +0.0792] exceeds 10.05) while eliminating
LLM token latency and API cost. The pooled 100-query
result (Hit@10 = 0.820) is driven by 50 trivial single-
hop controls (where both achieve 100%) and should not
be used as evidence for multi-hop parity.

V. LIMITATIONS AND THREATS TO VALIDITY
To facilitate objective peer assessment, we document the
critical limitations of this study:
1) Benchmark domain concentration: Our primary text
retrieval evaluations focus predominantly on a sin-
gle document-type family (retail receipts from SROIE,
N = 626) alongside scanned administrative forms from
FUNSD (N = 100) and natural images from MS-COCO
(N = 1,000). While receipt and form structures capture
common real-world OCR artifacts, document layouts
with multi-column prose, rich typography, or complex
financial tables may exhibit differing degradation dy-
2) Cross-engine and cross-domain OCR generalization:
While Apple Vision represents an advanced commer-
cial neural OCR system, replication across open-source
Tesseract 5.5 LSTM and deep neural EasyOCR 1.7.2
confirms that our headline findings (character n-gram re-
silience on verbatim optical noise and dense bi-encoder
collapse) replicate across distinct OCR architectures.
However, the ordering under light paraphrases exhibits
domain sensitivity: on retail receipts with entity sub-
stitutions, Word BM25 outperforms character BM25
across all three engines (Apple Clean: 0.4334 vs. 0.2427;
Tesseract: 0.3964 vs. 0.2265; EasyOCR: 0.3792 vs.
0.2292), whereas on administrative forms (FUNSD),
character BM25 retains a slight advantage (Apple Clean:
0.2228 vs. 0.1573; Tesseract: 0.2442 vs. 0.2019) due to
subword matching of compound form headers and layout
3) Conformal cascade calibration: Under marginal loss
L = 1|not escalated ^ Y ‡ 1], split conformal cal-
ibration reports an observed mean test miss risk of
0.0494 at a 78.4% escalation rate. Because the 200 splits
resample the same fixed pool of N = 2,754 instances,
the 95% CI of the mean risk [0.0480, 0.0502] describes
only the sample mean across partitions of this pool, not
a generalization CI for unseen queries or documents.
Empirical split coverage (risk ≤ 0.05) is only 58.5%,
below nominal 95% coverage, and equal-escalation fixed
margin achieves matching accuracy (0.3579 vs. 0.3577,
p > 0.05). Entity rewrites experience risk 0.0627 (>
0.05), demonstrating that marginal calibration does not
guarantee conditional protection per query type.
4) Answerable question formulation: Our answerable
questions evaluate natural factual queries isolating se-
mantic abstraction from lexical absence. However, real-
world user queries may exhibit broader syntactic and
conversational diversity.
5) LLM judge bias and audit sample size: Automated
diagnostic scoring uses gpt -40-mini [23], which car-
ries documented biases [24]. Mitigated by dual-reviewer
human auditing rated by the two co-authors (A. K. Ven-
nela and G. S. B. Koushik) across 110 cases (K = 0.8716
faithfulness, 0.8926 relevance, 0.9451 correctness, mean
K = 0.9031). While inter-annotator agreement is high,
expanding audits to external non-author panels remains

6) Multi-hop retrieval utility and exploratory power
limits: Query decomposition incurs a 45% latency
penalty (4,736.8 ms vs. 3,260.0 ms). Paired discordant
analysis across 50 multi-hop queries indicates that multi-
hop LLM bridging provides no statistically detectable
retrieval improvement over single-stage hybrid retrieval
(+1 net hit / 50; exact McNemar p = 1.000) or single-
stage dense retrieval (identical 32/50 hits). However,
at N = 50 paired queries, statistical power is limited
(minimum detectable difference > 10.0792, spanning
beyond 10.05), meaning formal statistical equivalence
cannot be claimed and this evaluation should be regarded
as exploratory.
7) Dose-response non-linearity: The retrieval drop under
query mismatch is non-monotonic across query types:
light paraphrases with entity substitutions trigger severe
drops (Apple Vision A = 0.4037 MRR; Tesseract
A = 0.3400), whereas answerable factual questions
preserve key topical anchors and sustain high lexical
retrieval (MRR = 0.9471).
8) Synthetic vs. optical noise divergence: Character n-
gram robustness and dictionary-based reliability weight-
ing tuned on synthetic character permutations fail to
translate directly to real optical OCR blur. System ar-
chitects must validate on physical optical degradation
rather than synthetic character noise.
9) LLM-generated query synthesis and single gen-
erator threat: Evaluation queries for light para-
phrases and answerable questions were synthesized us-
ing gpt-4o-mini [23]. No human-authored query set
was used. Because queries were generated using a single
LLM without multi-model cross-generation or human
validation, model-generated queries may under-represent
human typographical errors, spontaneous colloquialisms,
or ambiguous intent.
10) Dense and learned sparse model scope: Our evaluation
benchmarks representative widely deployed bi-encoders
(al1-MiniLM-L6-V2,
bge-base-en-v1.5).
Emerging models with multilingual subword tokenizers
BGE-M3), learned
sparse representations
(SPLADE), and token-level multi-vector text interaction
(ColBERTV2) represent compelling extensions for
future benchmark iterations.
VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this work, we have established that intermediate textual
proxies in multimodal retrieval-augmented generation exhibit
well-defined, regime-dependent efficacy boundaries rather than
uniform success or failure. Our empirical investigation across
1,626 multimodal items (SROIE, FUNSD, MS-COCO) reveals
three principal architectural insights.
First, lexical inverted indexing over character sub-words (n-
grams of length 3-5) provides a resilient sparse retrieval foun-
dation, outperforming standard word tokenization across both
commercial neural OCR and open-source Tesseract engines
under heavy optical blur (Apple Clean: 0.9436 vs. 0.8371;
Degraded: 0.8248 vs. 0.6972). This dominance reverses un-
der entity-substituting light paraphrases, where word BM25
(0.4334) surpasses character BM25 (0.2427). On FUNSD
forms, the verbatim margin narrows to +0.0069 (statistical
tie). Second, the frequently observed collapse of dense bi-
encoders on administrative text is associated with a query-span
formulation mismatch rather than sequence truncation; struc-
turing user queries as natural answerable questions improves
BGE-Base MRR from 0.3256 to 0.5263 on identical document
text. Third, native visual representations strongly outperform
intermediate machine caption proxies for unconstrained pho-
tographic imagery (SigLIP MRR 0.6071 vs. machine captions
0.3728, p < 10-4), with no significant difference detected
from human gold captions (0.5835, p = 0.142; equivalence
not tested); however, on structured document pages, document-
native ColQwen2 shows no significant difference from CPU
lexical search on answerable factual questions (p > 0.05)
while imposing 249.21 ms GPU latency vs. 0.87 ms CPU
verbatim (5.72 ms on answerable queries).
Conformal cascade calibration achieves mean test miss
risk 0.0494 on resampled splits of a finite pool (mean CI
[0.0480, 0.0502), includes 0.05) with 58.5% split coverage at
78.4% escalation; an equal-escalation fixed margin achieves
matching MRR (0.3579 vs. 0.3577). On the 50-query multi-
hop diagnostic suite, extractive PRF shows no detectable
difference from generative LLM bridging (Hit@10 0.640 vs.
0.640, p = 1.000; formal equivalence not established) with
zero API cost.
Future research will extend this regime framework along
three axes: (1) expanding held-out evaluation to multilingual
and handwritten administrative archives; (2) designing adap-
tive conformal thresholding conditioned on real-time query
difficulty estimators; and (3) investigating sparse-guided se-
lective caching for vision-language models. By formalizing
the trade-offs between computational overhead and represen-
tation fidelity, this work provides an engineering roadmap
for efficient, trustworthy multimodal retrieval in real-world
computing systems.

I. INTRODUCTION
The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia across
enterprise archives, digital libraries, and operational repos-
itories demands information retrieval systems capable of
searching records that are not natively textual. In enterprise
document workflows-such as healthcare systems digitizing
millions of paper patient intake records, legal firms archiving
scanned court proceedings, and supply chain enterprises in-
dexing procurement invoices-organizations process massive
volumes of unstructured physical records daily. Transforming
these documents into queryable digital assets is essential
for business intelligence, compliance auditing, and decision
support [4]. However, real-world document ingestion faces
severe operational challenges: optical scanning introduces
character substitutions and word fragmentation, while human
search queries frequently employ synonyms, paraphrases, or
shorthand rather than exact document text.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [3] addresses the
hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models (LLMs)
by grounding responses in retrieved domain documents. Re-
cently, multimodal extensions of RAG have emerged to handle
non-textual data, as comprehensively surveyed by Abootorabi
et al. [28]. For example, Patel et al. [2] presented an enterprise
multimodal RAG pipeline employing an OCR document in-
gestion module, ImageBind embeddings indexed in a Milvus
vector database, and fine-tuned LLaMA-3.
In a proxy-mediated design, three practical failure modes
remain important:
1) Single-Stage Dense Retrieval Pitfalls: Relying ex-
clusively on single-stage dense vector similarity per
turn can induce semantic drift. Dense embeddings may
overlook exact lexical tokens, numerical identifiers, item
codes, and proper nouns that sparse inverted indexes can
match directly 9].
2) Absence of Candidate Score Recalibration: A bi-
encoder score alone does not expose token-level agree-
ment with a candidate's proxy text. A lightweight
second-stage scorer can therefore be useful before con-
text assembly, even when it is not a neural cross-encoder.
3) Failure on Multi-Hop Queries Across Modalities: A
single retrieval pass does not ensure that a fact recovered
from one modality becomes a useful probe for another.
Iterative bridging can improve lexical reachability, but it
also introduces cascading extraction errors that must be
measured rather than assumed away.
To investigate these trade-offs, this paper presents a public-
benchmark regime analysis of text-proxy retrieval across held-
out evaluation splits'.

II. RELATED WORK
A. Multimodal Representation and Retrieval
Early cross-modal retrieval systems relied on dual-encoder
contrastive learning. Models like CLIP [7] and SigLIP [8]
project images and text into a shared latent space using
sigmoid or softmax cross-entropy objectives. ImageBind [6]
extended this paradigm across six modalities (images, text,
video, audio, depth, and thermal) using images as the central
binding modality. While effective for broad semantic match-
ing, dual-encoders compress multimedia into fixed-dimension
vectors, frequently losing granular lexical and structural to-
kens. Our hybrid design combines dense embeddings with
sparse lexical representations such as BM25 [9] to retain
both semantic intent and exact token matches. Unlike single-
modality dual-encoders that discard fine-grained lexical iden-
tifiers, our framework analyzes the complementary regime
boundaries where character-level sparse indexing outperforms
dense representations under optical noise.
B. Multimodal RAG and Document Analysis
Integrating multimodal inputs into RAG workflows has
gained rapid momentum with the emergence of Vision-
Language Models (VLMs) and advanced LLMs. Recent native
multimodal document retrievers such as ColPali [26] and
M3DocRAG [27], benchmarked on the Visual Document
Retrieval (ViDoRe) suite [36], index document pages using
multi-vector vision-language representations to bypass optical
character recognition. While promising, multi-vector VLM
representations require substantial GPU memory and heavy
cross-attention compute during query serving. Conversely,
enterprise systems such as Patel et al. [2] and Joshi et al. [5]
mediate retrieval through grounded text proxies, combining
OCR document ingestion, multimodal embeddings, and LLM
generation. Our work investigates this text-proxy paradigm:
we evaluate the empirical trade-offs of hybrid dense-sparse
fusion, candidate scoring, and iterative query decomposition,
systematically delineating where text proxies excel and where
native visual representations remain necessary. Unlike ColPali
[26] which mandates multi-vector VLM computation for every
candidate page regardless of query complexity, our regime

analysis establishes the exact conditions under which sub-
millisecond CPU text proxies match or exceed native vision
models, identifying when GPU-heavy inference is truly justi-
fied.
C. Multi-Hop Reasoning in Retrieval Systems
Multi-hop retrieval addresses queries where no single doc-
ument contains the complete answer [11], [13]. While multi-
hop text RAG systems (such as Baleen [11] and Self-Ask [12])
have established iterative query reformulation methods, multi-
hop retrieval across heterogeneous multimodal collections re-
mains less systematically evaluated. Our diagnostic targets the
case in which the second-hop keyword is absent from the
original query and must be recovered from first-hop proxy
context; it does not claim that all multimodal QA benchmarks
assume co-located evidence. Unlike prior multi-hop pipelines
that rely on expensive generative LLMs for every hop, we
empirically show that rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance
feedback achieves parity in retrieval reachability with zero
generative token latency or API cost.
D. Adaptive Fusion, Cascade Ranking, and Selective Rerank-
ing
In information retrieval, static fusion coefficients fail to
account for query-level variance. Query Performance Predic-
tion (QPP) [29] and adaptive fusion techniques dynamically
adjust interpolation weights between sparse and dense scores
based on query ambiguity or lexical specificity. Similarly,
cascade ranking architectures [30], [31] balance retrieval
efficiency and ranking precision by passing top candidates
through successively more expressive models. In monomodal
web search, cascades evaluate candidates using fixed score
thresholds or supervised early-exit classifiers. However, ex-
isting cascade rankers do not account for multimodal proxy
corruption (e.g., OCR or ASR transcription noise) or cross-
modal query routing. As summarized in Table II, we formulate
and empirically evaluate candidate mechanisms-including
surface-feature query routing, confidence-margin cascades
(41,2 < Tmargin), and observable proxy reliability discounting
(rm (d))-to determine whether lightweight heuristic defenses
provide measurable utility over standard inverted indexes. Un-
like prior cascade ranking that relies on uncalibrated heuristic
margins, we ground cascade escalation in distribution-free
conformal risk control to guarantee test-set error bounds.
E. Optical Character Recognition Quality and Information
Retrieval
Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems translate
physical document imagery into digital character sequences,
but practical scanning routinely introduces character substi-
tutions, insertions, deletions, and bounding-box permutations
[14], [17]. Foundational information retrieval studies have es-
tablished that standard word-level tokenizers (such as inverted
indexes using whitespace and punctuation delimiters) suffer
catastrophic vocabulary mismatch when typographical errors
fracture keyword strings. Early mitigation strategies, including
Otsu thresholding [15] and Hough transforms [16] for skew
correction, focused on image-domain preprocessing to boost
OCR accuracy. However, in downstream information retrieval,
post-OCR lexical degradation leads to subword tokenization
fragmentation in subword-based language models and word
omissions in lexical indexes. Unlike prior works that treat
OCR error as an unmodeled uniform noise channel, our regime
analysis systematically evaluates character n-gram represen-
tations against word-level BM25 and neural cross-encoders
across both commercial and open-source OCR engines under
F. Conformal Prediction and Risk-Controlled Cascades
In mission-critical information retrieval, deploying neural
cross-encoders or multi-vector Vision-Language Models for
every candidate query imposes unsustainable serving latency
and energy expenditure. Cascade ranking pipelines address
this bottleneck by evaluating candidates through tiered stages,
escalating to expressive neural models only when prelimi-
nary scores indicate ranking ambiguity [30], [31]. However,
conventional cascade systems rely on empirical score mar-
gins or heuristic thresholds that offer no formal statistical
guarantees on retrieval accuracy. Conformal prediction, for-
mulated by Bates et al. [37] and surveyed by Angelopoulos
and Bates [38], provides a distribution-free, finite-sample
framework for bounding user-specified risk metrics without
restrictive distributional assumptions. By framing the decision
to escalate candidates as a risk-controlling prediction problem,
conformal prediction enables retrieval systems to bound the
probability of unescalated retrieval errors strictly below a pre-
specified tolerance a. In this work, we ground production cas-
cade ranking in finite-sample marginal conformal risk control,
establishing rigorous mathematical miss-rate guarantees while
reducing computational costs.

IV. EMPIRICAL REGIME ANALYSIS OF SPARSE, DENSE,
AND NATIVE-VISUAL RETRIEVAL UNDER PROXY NOISE
To evaluate the empirical boundaries of text-proxy retrieval
without annotation leakage, we benchmarked an expanded
public multimodal collection under a rigorous pre-specified
experimental protocol across held-out evaluation splits. We
structure our evaluation across three canonical operational
regimes:
• Regime A (Text-Dominated): Scanned receipts and ad-
ministrative forms evaluated under real optical character
recognition (ICDAR 2019 SROIE [32] and FUNSD [34]),
isolating sub-word lexical dominance, micro-mechanisms
of dense collapse, and production reranking cascades.
• Regime B (Visual-Dominated): Photographic scene
search under synthetic caption proxies (N = 1,000 MS-
COCO Karpathy test images [33]), establishing where
native vision-language embeddings decisively surpass
machine-generated text representations.
• Regime C (Cross-Modal and Multi-Hop): Composi-
tional relational queries spanning modalities, establishing
where rule-based extractive pseudo-relevance feedback
matches iterative generative LLM bridging without API
overhead.
Preliminary feasibility pilots over internal personal album pho-
tos and synthetic noise sweeps are documented in Appendix A.

To evaluate whether proxy corruption or semantic query
mismatch is the dominant bottleneck in text-proxy RAG,
we conducted exploratory paired permutation tests (perm
100,000). In the reconciled dose-response artifact (Table III
and Table XII), moving from verbatim lookups to light para-
phrasing on proprietary Apple Vision OCR collapses Word
BM25 by A = 0.4037 MRR (0.8371 to 0.4334), substantially
exceeding optical blur degradation (4 = 0.1399, 0.8371 to
0.6972, paired permutation p < 10-5). However, under open-
source Tesseract 5.5 OCR, optical blur collapses Word BM25
by 0.3916 MRR (0.7364 to 0.3448), which is comparable
in magnitude to the semantic paraphrase drop on clean text
(0.3400 MRR, 0.7364 to 0.3964). Thus, semantic paraphrase
mismatch dominates mild-to-moderate OCR noise, but severe
optical blur induces comparable or greater retrieval collapse.
System builders must balance query-side reformulation with
robust sub-word indexing.

To verify whether this dense degradation is an artifact
of sequence length truncation, we evaluated token length
distributions across all 626 SROIE receipts. While only 4
receipts (0.64%) exceed 512 tokens, the real parameter limit
for al1-MiniLM-L6-v2 is max_seq_length = 256, where
209 of 626 receipts (33.39%) exceed 256 WordPiece tokens.
However, evaluating chunked MaxP retrieval across 150-word

identical MRR to unchunked single-vector retrieval (MiniLM:

chunked vs. 0.3022 unchunked), demonstrating that sequence
truncation is not the primary cause of dense collapse.

queries as natural answerable questions improves BGE-Base
MRR to 0.5263 (Hit@10 79.74%) on the identical uncorrupted
document text. Dense bi-encoders are trained on natural lan-
guage asymmetric question-passage pairs; when queries mirror

Furthermore, to establish the causal impact of tokenization
fragmentation versus query formulation, we evaluated a vo-
cabulary projection intervention against the clean Dev lexi-
con under 20% character noise. Reconstructing broken word
tokens restored 65.3% of the induced WordPiece subword

MRR). These results support the interpretation that query
formulation mismatch explains weak dense performance on
clean text, while subword tokenization fragmentation explains
the additional performance drop under noise.

critical limitations of this study:
1) Benchmark domain concentration: Our primary text
retrieval evaluations focus predominantly on a sin-
gle document-type family (retail receipts from SROIE,
N = 626) alongside scanned administrative forms from
FUNSD (N = 100) and natural images from MS-COCO
(N = 1,000). While receipt and form structures capture
common real-world OCR artifacts, document layouts
with multi-column prose, rich typography, or complex
financial tables may exhibit differing degradation dy-
2) Cross-engine OCR generalization: While Apple Vi-
sion represents an advanced commercial neural OCR
system, replication across open-source Tesseract 5.5
LSTM confirms that our architectural findings (character
n-gram robustness and dense collapse) replicate across
distinct OCR model architectures and error distributions.
3) Conformal cascade calibration: Under marginal loss

Multi-hop retrieval utility and latency overhead:
Query decomposition incurs a 45% latency penalty
(4,736.8 ms vs. 3,260.0 ms). Paired discordant analy-

8) Synthetic vs. optical noise divergence: Character n-
gram robustness and dictionary-based reliability weight-

translate directly to real optical OCR blur. System ar-

rather than synthetic character noise.
9) LLM-generated query synthesis and single gen-

erator threat: Evaluation queries for light para-
phrases and answerable questions were synthesized us-

LLM without multi-model cross-generation or human
validation, model-generated queries may under-represent

or ambiguous intent.
VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
In this work, we have established that intermediate textual
proxies in multimodal retrieval-augmented generation exhibit
well-defined, regime-dependent efficacy boundaries rather than
uniform success or failure. Our empirical investigation across
1,626 multimodal items reveals three principal architectural
insights.
First, lexical inverted indexing over character sub-words
(n-grams of length 3-5) provides an extraordinarily resilient
sparse retrieval foundation, outperforming standard word to-
kenization across both commercial neural OCR and open-
source engines under heavy optical blur; whole-word and
dense encoders only surpass sub-word sparse matching when
search queries diverge into semantic paraphrases. Second,
the frequently observed collapse of dense bi-encoders on
administrative text reflects a query-span formulation mismatch
rather than sequence truncation; structuring user queries as
contextual answerable questions restores semantic discrim-
inability without modifying document vectors. Third, native
visual representations are indispensable for unconstrained pho-
tographic imagery, where automated caption proxies suffer se-
vere information bottlenecks; however, on structured document
pages, document-native vision-language models yield statisti-
cally indistinguishable accuracy from CPU lexical search on
factual questions while imposing two orders of magnitude
higher latency.
These findings directly challenge the emerging assump-
tion that end-to-end multi-vector vision models must uni-
versally replace OCR-mediated indexing. Instead, we show
that lightweight sub-word lexical inverted indexes on CPU
remain optimal for high-throughput verbatim and entity-centric
search, while cross-encoder cascades should be reserved selec-
tively for paraphrased queries via conformal risk control. Fur-
thermore, rule-based extractive entity bridging matches multi-
hop generative LLM techniques without incurring recurring
token latency or cloud API costs.
Future research will extend this regime framework along
three axes: (1) expanding held-out evaluation to multilingual
and handwritten administrative archives; (2) designing adap-
tive conformal thresholding conditioned on real-time query
designine
difficulty estimators; and (3) investigating sparse-guided selec-
tive caching for vision-language models. By formalizing the
trade-offs between computational overhead and representation
fidelity, this work provides a rigorous engineering roadmap
for efficient, trustworthy multimodal retrieval in real-world
computing systems.

I. Introduction
The rapid proliferation of heterogeneous multimedia
across enterprise archives, digital libraries, and operational
repositories demands information retrieval systems capa-
ble of searching records that are not natively textual.
Modern knowledge workflows frequently require querying
across diverse media types such as scanned forms, audio
recordings, and photographic archives while preserving
exact names, identifiers, and category labels [4].
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) 3] addresses
the hallucination tendencies of Large Language Models
(LLMs) by grounding responses in retrieved domain doc-
uments. Recently, multimodal extensions of RAG have
emerged to handle non-textual data, as comprehensively
surveyed by Abootorabi et al. [28]. For example, Patel et
al. [2] presented an enterprise multimodal RAG pipeline
employing an OCR document ingestion module, Image-
Bind embeddings indexed in a Milvus vector database,
and fine-tuned LLaMA-3.
In a proxy-mediated design, three practical failure
modes remain important:
1) Single-Stage Dense Retrieval Pitfalls: Relying exclu-
sively on single-stage dense vector similarity per turn
can induce semantic drift. Dense embeddings may
overlook exact lexical tokens, numerical identifiers,
item codes, and proper nouns that sparse inverted
indexes can match directly 9].
Absence of Candidate Score Recalibration: A
bi-encoder score alone does not expose token-
level agreement with a candidate's proxy text. A
lightweight second-stage scorer can therefore be
useful before context assembly, even when it is not
a neural cross-encoder.
3) Failure on Multi-Hop Queries Across Modalities:
A single retrieval pass does not ensure that a
fact recovered from one modality becomes a useful
probe for another. Iterative bridging can improve
lexical reachability, but it also introduces cascading
extraction errors that must be measured rather than
assumed away.
To investigate these trade-offs, this paper presents a
text-proxy-grounded multi-stage, multi-hop Multimodal
RAG architecture and evaluates the empirical valid-
ity of adaptive fusion, query routing, and reliability
weighting under a pre-specified analysis plan (commit
97d4ab56, frozen 2026-10-25; repository branch: research,
released for camera-ready publication at https://github.
com/koushik2109/Memory Verse/tree/research).
